Overview
This course is for anyone with a basic knowledge of R who wants to improve their programming. Each session is hands-on: you work through practical examples that apply what you have learned, with plenty of support for your questions and anything you get stuck on.

title: Advancing in R
text:
How to use this book
For many of the chapters, we will provide the code you need to use. You can copy and paste from the book using the clipboard in the top-right corner.
We also provide the solutions to many of the activities. No-one is going to check whether you tried to figure it out yourself rather than going straight to the solution, but remember this: if you copy and paste without thinking, you will learn nothing.
Finally, we update the book from time to time, fixing typos and adding detail or activities, so treat it as a living document. Please tell us if you find any mistakes.

Framing and mental models
Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. To see how one works inside, you build a small one yourself in Block 6.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
section: What is a large language model?
text:
What is a large language model?
A large language model predicts the next fragment of text from what came before, having learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist, so if a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, switching is a cheap experiment.

title: Block 1: AI-assisted R programming
text:
Why the context window matters
An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have; because they are only requests, Block 5 adds controls that hold either way, and tests check the result.
Remember: the AI sees only what you give it, and everything it sees has left your machine.

text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipWhich tool does what







Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron, which starts in your project’s root folder: the folder it acts on. Every block’s main text uses it, and checks its work from the R console and Git pane.

Posit Assistant is the in-IDE chat and agent in RStudio and Positron. It can also see your live R session. See What’s new in Posit AI.

GitHub Copilot gives inline completions in RStudio and Positron. Its cloud agent, used only in some Going further sections, needs a paid plan; see the Copilot plans page.










TipModels





Claude Code uses Anthropic’s Claude models; Posit Assistant runs on Posit AI or a provider key you configure; GitHub Copilot offers Claude, GPT and Gemini models. You do not need strong opinions about which model is best, only to know that the choice exists and changes the output.









TipTwo modes of execution





The tools you use today are synchronous and local: they work on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted. Their reach differs: the current file for inline completion, the project folder and the output of its own commands for Claude Code, and your live R session too for Posit Assistant. An asynchronous, remote agent, such as the Copilot cloud agent, works on its own branch on someone else’s servers and returns a pull request minutes later; you meet it in the Going further sections of Blocks 3, 5 and 8. The first invites you to watch and interrupt; the second, to write a precise specification and review what comes back. Block 3 turns this into a ladder of autonomy.









TipThe thread, in more detail





Day 1 introduced renv; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs (TADA! and the README, and the SORTEE checklist); Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use, and a log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later.

Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


characterisation test
A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.

Step 1: Open the Terminal tab in your IDE


RStudio: the Terminal tab next to the Console.

Positron: Terminal → New Terminal.

With a project open, the Terminal tab starts in the project’s root folder, which is where Claude Code needs to run. You never need to cd.
Which shell is it? A prompt starting PS is PowerShell (Windows); one ending $ is Git Bash (Windows) or bash/zsh (macOS, Linux).

section: Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
text:
Step 2: Check git and R are reachable
In the terminal:
git --version
Rscript --version
Both should print a version number.


git not found: install git (on Windows, Git for Windows).

Rscript not found (common on Windows): run R.home("bin") in the R console and add that folder to your PATH (Windows: Start menu → “Edit environment variables for your account” → Path). Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron: its terminals keep the PATH they started with.

title: Setting up Claude Code
text:
Step 3: Install Claude Code
macOS or Linux, in the terminal:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows, in PowerShell (a prompt starting PS; if your Terminal tab is Git Bash, open the PowerShell app for this one step):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Then quit and reopen RStudio or Positron, and check the version in the Terminal tab:
claude --version
You are done when it prints 2.1.281 or later. This minimum is about your instruction file: by this version, Claude Code reads your AGENTS.md directly and lists it in /memory.

text:
Step 5: Sign in
With your workshop repository open, type claude in its Terminal tab. On first launch a browser window opens: sign in with your account (/logout and /login switch accounts later). If a Terminal tab was open before you switched projects, close it and open a new one.






WarningUsing an API key

Step 7: An API key for Block 6
In Block 6 you build your own agent in R with the ellmer package. It calls Claude through the Anthropic API, which is billed per request and is separate from a Claude Pro or Max subscription.

Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


permission mode
The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).


skill
A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


symbolic link
A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.

text:
Exercise 1: A logic error
AI is a fast debugging partner for code you wrote yourself, because you can judge its answer against what you meant. You fix two bugs that raise no error: one the data reveal, and one that only your knowledge of the study catches.

text:
Setup
Create this block’s practice script, and load the voles data in it. This command creates the scratch/ folder and the script, and opens it:
In the R console:

usethis::edit_file("scratch/debugging.R")

In scratch/debugging.R:

library(tidyverse)

Run these lines. In each exercise, paste the code shown below them, run it to see the problem, and fix it there.
How you use Claude Code in this block. Claude Code is an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.: given a question, it may search your project, read files and offer to run code. Apart from the last step of Exercise 1, you only ask: you gather the evidence and paste it in. So:

type /clear where an exercise tells you to: it starts a new conversation, so nothing from the previous one carries over;
end each prompt with “Answer from what I’ve pasted: don’t read files, run code or edit anything.” Without it, Claude Code may read your files to gather evidence itself. The line is only a request: Claude Code has no ask mode, and plan mode is not used here because it still reads your files while it plans;
if it still asks to run a command or edit a file, choose No. Manual mode means it must ask first, and your answer is the control.

Claude Code cannot see the objects in your R console, such as voles: it sees your data only by reading files or running code, and each Rscript command it runs starts a fresh R process. Check its work in the R console (checking work).

TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant: type /ask first. Ask mode is read-only: it cannot edit files or run R code, so the answer-only line is not needed. It does see the names and types of the objects in your session (not their values) and can read your console history, so it may already have your distinct() output: that is a disclosure route too (Block 3). For step 3 of Exercise 1, type /normal so it can run the diagnostics in your live R session, approving each call; /normal is also how you leave Ask mode.

title: Block 2: Debugging with AI
text:
A logic error (12 minutes)


Goal: find a bug that raises no error by inspecting the data first, so that you can check the agent’s diagnosis against evidence you have seen yourself.
Start state: your workshop repository on main; Claude Code in Manual mode, with a new conversation (/clear).






TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant: type /ask first. Ask mode is read-only: it cannot edit files or run R code, so the answer-only line is not needed. It does see the names and types of the objects in your session (not their values) and can read your console history, so it may already have your distinct() output: that is a disclosure route too (Block 3). For step 4, type /normal so it can run the diagnostics in your live R session, approving each call; /normal is also how you leave Ask mode.
A chat window: paste the same prompts, without the answer-only line, and skip step 4.



1. Set up. In the R console, usethis::edit_file("scratch/debugging.R") creates this block’s practice script and opens it. Paste this in and run it; the last two commands are code you wrote to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles:

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
voles <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))

high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

It runs without error but returns NaN: the bug is in what you asked for, so put the evidence in front of you first, then in front of the assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files..
2. Inspect the data before asking for help. In the R console:

voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)
voles |> count(treatment_arm)
nrow(high_dose)

The values are Control, Low_dose and High_dose, and nrow() is zero: you have found the bug yourself in seconds.
3. Ask with the evidence in hand. Paste the code and the diagnostic output together, so that the answer rests on the real values, not a guess.
Prompt (Claude Code):
I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles.
My code:

  high_dose <- voles |>
    filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose")

  high_dose |>
    summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g))

returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns
"Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of
the capitalisation. Is that the only problem?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
If it asks to run a command or edit a file despite the last line, choose No. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Ignore a first line # agents-md: active v1 in its code: Block 4 explains it.






NoteHow it works: asking an agent only to answer





Claude Code is an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.: given a question, it may search your project, read files and offer to run code. The answer-only line is only a request: Claude Code has no ask mode, and plan mode is not used here because it still reads your files while it plans. Manual mode is the control: it must ask before it runs a command or edits a file, and your answer decides.
Claude Code cannot see the objects in your R console, such as voles: it sees your data only by reading files or running code, and each Rscript command it runs starts a fresh R process. Check its work in the R console (checking work).



4. Now let the agent gather the evidence. This is the one step in the block where it acts. Type /clear, so that it starts without the evidence you pasted, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and run R code with Rscript to find why
filtering treatment_arm for "high_dose" returns no rows. Don't edit any files.
Show each command and its output.
It reads the file without asking (reading needs no approval), but asks before it runs R. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can, so choose Yes if the Rscript command only reads the data and prints results. Then compare its diagnosis with yours from step 2.
Keep this conversation open: in Block 3 you read its transcript to see what reached the model provider.


Solution


high_dose <- voles |>
  filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose")

high_dose |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE))

The filter now matches the data. na.rm = TRUE is a precaution for real data, which usually have missing values.

You are done when nrow(high_dose) is 24, the mean is a number, not NaN, and the agent’s diagnosis in step 4 matches yours from step 2.
If it goes wrong: if nrow() is still zero, run voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) again and copy the value exactly as printed.

section: Exercise 2: A correct-looking but wrong result
text:
Exercise 2: A correct-looking but wrong result


A correct-looking but wrong result (8 minutes)


Goal: catch a result that runs cleanly but is wrong by stating the expected answer before you ask, so that a plausible but wrong number does not reach your results.
Start state: scratch/debugging.R is open with voles loaded. Ask in Exercise 1’s conversation, without /clear, so that its transcript is still there for Block 3.
You wrote this to get the mean change in body mass by treatment arm. Paste it into scratch/debugging.R and run it:

voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

It runs, and the numbers look plausible. But the treatment was designed to increase mass, and they say mass falls. Only your knowledge of the study reveals the error: an AI catches it only if you tell it what the answer should be.
1. Write down what a correct result should look like, then compare. Here: positive values, rising from Control to High_dose. The mismatch is the diagnosis.
2. Ask for a second opinion, stating the expected direction.
Prompt (Claude Code):
This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative
and decreasing. What is wrong?

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |>
    summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.


Solution


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm)

mass_change_g is post minus pre: gain, not loss. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction.

You are done when your corrected means are positive and increase from Control to High_dose, as you predicted in step 1.
If it goes wrong: if the values are still negative, check which mass you subtract from which: post minus pre is gain.








NoteThe debugging checklist





Inspect the data first, ask the AI second.


Read the error in full: the function name and the phrase usually locate the bug.

Inspect the data: glimpse(), distinct(), summary(), and nrow() after a filter.

Check names exactly, including capitals and underscores.

Then ask, giving the code, the error and the diagnostic output together. Ask for an answer, not an action, until you have the evidence.

Explain the fix in one sentence before you accept it.

Before trusting a clean run, state what the result should look like (sign, size, order) and compare.










NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: use an assistant to diagnose and fix errors in your own code, trusted because you inspect the data first and explain each fix in a sentence.

Check: before trusting a clean run, state the sign and size the result should have, and compare.

TipA misspelt function name (self-study)





Goal: fix an error with Claude Code’s help and explain the fix in one sentence, so that you accept only a fix you understand.
Start state: scratch/debugging.R is open with voles loaded, and Claude Code has a new conversation (/clear). During the workshop, wait until after Block 3, which reads Exercise 1’s conversation.
You wrote this in scratch/debugging.R to count voles per treatment:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_barchart()

R returns:
Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"
1. Ask for a fix. Paste the code and the error, and ask.
Prompt (Claude Code):
This code gives an error:

  ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
    geom_barchart()

Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart"

What is wrong, and what is the fix?
Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything.
2. Explain it before you accept it. Write one sentence saying why the original failed. If you can write it, you understood the fix; that sentence is your check.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_bar()

The function is geom_bar(); ggplot2’s geoms have no _chart suffix. This is not a syntax error: R parses the code without complaint, and fails only when it looks for a function called geom_barchart() and finds none. “Could not find function” means no loaded package has a function of that name.

You are done when the corrected plot draws a bar for each treatment arm, and you have written your one-sentence explanation.
If it goes wrong: if the fix produces a different error, paste that error back in the same conversation; the assistant now has two clues.









TipAn aesthetic-mapping error





This error needs ggplot2’s grammar rather than the data. You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm:

ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(color = treatment_arm) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

R returns an error saying that object treatment_arm was not found. The exact wording varies between ggplot2 versions.
1. Ask for a fix. Before accepting it, write one sentence on why ggplot2 could not find treatment_arm.


Solution


ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) +
  labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass")

treatment_arm is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside aes(). An argument outside aes(), such as color =, expects a fixed value like "red" or "#0072B2". ggplot2 looked for an object called treatment_arm in your environment, found none, and stopped. colour and color are interchangeable in ggplot2.

When ggplot2 reports that a column such as treatment_arm was not found, the most common cause is:

The data argument was supplied incorrectlyA column name was used outside aes(), where ggplot2 expected a fixed valueThe ggplot2 package is not loadedThe variable contains missing values

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
section: Part A: What can the assistant see?
text:
Part A: What can the assistant see?
An assistant’s answer about your data is reliable only when it has real information: something you pasted, a file it read, or output from a command it ran. In Block 2 you mostly pasted that information yourself; once, you let the agent fetch it on its own. Either way, everything it uses leaves your machine.
Exercise 1: Name the routes


Name the routes (3 minutes)


Goal: see exactly what reached the model provider when the agent investigated in Block 2, so that you can name every route your data take.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, and Claude Code running in the Terminal tab, as you left it in Block 2.
1. Find the transcript. Scroll back in Claude Code to the transcript of Block 2’s Exercise 1, where the agent read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and ran Rscript. Above each reply, Claude Code lists the actions it took. If you cleared it, re-run that prompt from Block 2.
2. Name each route. For each action, name its route in the diagram below: a file it read is route 2; the output of a command it ran is route 4; what you pasted yourself, in Exercise 2’s prompt, is route 1. Add one file that no action shows: AGENTS.md, which Claude Code reads at the start of every conversation, also by route 2.
You are done when you can name every file or command output that reached the model provider.
If it goes wrong: if the transcript shows files you did not expect, or a search of the project, name those too: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below matter for confidential data.


Disclosure: every route out of your machine
Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider, by four routes:



Route 1: what you paste


Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt


any tool


Model provider




Route 2: files it reads


Copilot: open files. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: any project file they choose to read


read


Model provider




Route 3: session context the IDE injects


Your live R session: R version, and the names and types of your objects (not their values)


Posit Assistant only


Model provider




Route 4: output of commands it runs


The agent runs Rscript or head data.csv, and reads what it prints


Claude Code, Posit Assistant


Model provider



Everything before an arrow reaches the model provider. A data file in the project may already be disclosed; for a tibble loaded in your session, its names and types are, and its values as soon as code the agent runs prints them.








ImportantWorking with confidential data: five habits





Work on a copy. Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s folder.

Know your account. Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training; on Pro or Max, set /privacy-settings. Check your institution’s approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.

Deny reads of sensitive folders in /permissions, for example Read(/data/confidential/**). It stops Claude Code’s own file reads and simple commands such as cat, but not R code that opens the file itself.

Stay in Manual mode, and refuse any command that would print records.

Describe, don’t show. names() gives column names and summary() the shape of the data; print(), glimpse() and str() show actual values.







TipBackground: tool-specific notes





There is no .claudeignore file, and /sandbox is not available on native Windows. Posit Assistant blocks .Renviron and .env by default, and shares the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs can still print values.





Context you hold in your head
A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your instructor may show this with two prompts; the demonstration is below, and you can try it yourself in Going further.






TipInstructor: demonstration





Your instructor asks a new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
and then, in another new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision.

Part B: What can the assistant do?
The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).: what it may do without asking. Each level is a rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. on an autonomy ladder. From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool calls run without your approval. Block 6, after lunch, builds that approval step in code.








Rung
What happens
Claude Code
Posit Assistant



0. Suggest
Completes the line you are typing
—
Next Edit Suggestions


1. Ask
Answers; changes nothing
— (no ask mode; Block 2’s answer-only line is a request)

2. Plan

Your starting mode. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual, although recent versions of Claude Code start in auto; keep Manual for confidential data. /plan can still run commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the quick reference has the rest.
Rung 3 is where routine work is safe, for example adding a derived column and a plot script. Three things make it safe: you start from a commit, so any change can be reverted; every edit and command is shown to you first; and a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports. Exercise 2 is exactly this.






NoteThe safe vibe-coding recipe





Commit, so you start from a clean Git pane.

Protect the inputs: /permissions shows the deny rules, or you add one.

Have the checks ready: tests in tests/ before the agent starts.

Ask in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.

Run the checks: the test suite in a fresh R session.

Read the diff in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 8; the template ships the protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there.








Warning



Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action: in acceptEdits, for example, file commands such as cp and mv run without asking, so a cp over a raw data file needs no approval.


The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions, which is why Block 4 writes them down.
Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy


Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)


Goal: have the agent add a column and a plot script at rung 3, then check its work with the diff and the tests, so that you trust the change because you checked it, not because the agent reported it.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab. Check its work from the R console and the Git pane (checking work).
1. Plan (rung 2). In Claude Code, type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g) to the voles data frame itself. Create a new script
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that plots mass_change_g by
treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/ with ggsave(). Don't run
anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
Before approving, check the plan names both files, adds the column to voles itself, leaves data/raw/ alone and saves the figure to outputs/. If anything is missing, choose No, keep planning and say what to change.
2. Act, with approval (rung 3). Choose Yes, manually approve edits, so it stays in Manual mode, and read each edit before you approve it. The repository’s AGENTS.md tells it to run new scripts, so it may still ask to run Rscript: choose No.
A rule for every approval today: approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now. Here you don’t, because you check the result yourself next; refusing is always safe.
3. Read the diff. Click Diff in the Git pane for each changed file and read it as you would a colleague’s work: the diff shows every change, including any you did not ask for.
4. Record. Create docs/ai-log.md (usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")) and write the first line of your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1. Use today’s date, written as YYYY-MM-DD:
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
You will add a line after each block in which an agent works. Writing it before you test means the next step checks it too.
5. Test, then commit. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so nothing left in your session can make a test pass, and run:
In the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_explore.R checks that mass_change_g in voles really is post minus pre, and runs the plot script in a fresh R session to check a figure arrived in outputs/. test_ai_log.R checks your log line has four parts separated by semicolons and a real date. Tests for later blocks skip. Commit the log and both scripts together; git ignores outputs/, so the figure stays out of the commit, and the plot script can make it again.
You are done when you have read every line of the diff, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your first AI-use log line is committed with both scripts.
If it goes wrong: select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click Revert, then ask again more clearly. If test_explore.R says voles has no mass_change_g, the agent made the column somewhere else: ask it to add the column to voles itself. Out of time? The checkpoint-skills branch, at the end of Block 4, holds this block’s files.






TipStretch: reflect on the rungs





At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff?
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')".











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, trusted because you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result.

Check: the Git pane’s diff after every agent action; the agent’s report that something “still runs” is a claim until a test confirms it.

Reproduce: work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert.

Record: your AI-use log starts here, in docs/ai-log.md.

Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


permission mode
The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.

text:
Activity 1: Make AGENTS.md yours
You write your conventions down once, so that every conversation follows them: in an instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees., which loads every time, and in a skillA folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description., which loads only when needed. Both are requests the model usually follows; Block 5 covers rules that always hold.
⏱ ~35 minutes · Start on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Part A: Instructions
Your conventions live in one file, AGENTS.md, at the repository root. Claude Code reads it at the start of every conversation because the template ships no CLAUDE.md; creating one (for example with /init) would hide your conventions.



Instruction file: loaded into every conversation


AGENTS.md: your conventions


read by


Claude Code




Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant


.agents/skills/<your-skill>/ (the master copy)


you copy


.claude/skills/<your-skill>/


read by


Claude Code



The course’s own skills already ship in both folders; Part B shows how to copy one you write.


Instructions that work are:


one per line, and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”);

true of your own code, or the model gets mixed signals;

short, because the file loads into every request;

added when a mistake repeats: a correction in chat is forgotten next conversation;

not guarantees: “never edit raw data” belongs here and in the enforced controls of Block 5.

Activity 1: Make AGENTS.md yours
Your workshop repository already contains a starter AGENTS.md. Make it describe your practice, then prove that Claude Code reads it.






NoteThe starter AGENTS.md





It includes a canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.: a fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you can see the file was loaded. The “Tests” rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit, which later blocks rely on.


# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Before you report a task done, run each new script once with Rscript from
  the project root and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- Before you report a task done, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')"
  once and paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Version control
- Before you edit any file, run git status.
- If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up.
- If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to
  commit first.
- Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. The one
  exception: a skill may run tests/make_reference.R once, to capture a
  reference that does not exist yet.







Edit, check, verify (12 minutes)


Goal: make AGENTS.md describe your own practice and prove Claude Code loads it, so that every later conversation starts from your conventions.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab (checking work).
1. Baseline. See the starter file at work before you change it.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot
of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not
create any files.
Look for the canary, # agents-md: active v1, as the first line of the code. (Asking for the code in the reply gives the canary somewhere to appear.)
2. Make it yours. Type /memory, choose AGENTS.md, and in your editor:

delete one rule you do not actually follow;
add one convention you always follow.

Keep the canary and the Tests, Statistics, Version control and Working with me sections: later blocks rely on them, and tests/test_controls.R checks for the canary and the git status line. Save.
3. Verify. Type /clear and repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was loaded; check the plot code against your new rule to see whether it was followed.
4. Check it with a test. In the R console, after Session → Restart R:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_controls.R confirms AGENTS.md is in place with its canary and git status rule, the project still starts in Manual mode, and the deny rules are intact. Commit AGENTS.md from the Git pane.
You are done when the canary appears, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your edited AGENTS.md is committed.
If it goes wrong: check that /memory lists AGENTS.md. Claude Code reads it because the template ships no CLAUDE.md; if you created one, delete it. If test_controls.R fails, restore the canary or the git status line. A failure in test_explore.R or test_ai_log.R is left over from Block 3: fix it there. Still stuck? Compare with the checkpoint-skills branch from the Git pane’s branch menu.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Part B: Skills
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file, plus any scripts or templates it needs. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., between two lines of three dashes at the top, gives a name and a description:


The description is the trigger. “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. Invoking it by name (/skill-name) always works.

The body is a procedure: when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check. It loads only when used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md.







TipBackground: skills that run only by name





For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



Where skills live. Write a skill in .agents/skills/<name>/, then copy it to .claude/skills/<name>/ for Claude Code, and again whenever you change it. The course’s own skills already ship in both; type /skills to list them.
In the R console:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)







NoteWhy two folders?





.agents/skills/ is the master copy, which other tools such as Posit Assistant read directly; Claude Code reads .claude/skills/. The deny rules keep the agent’s edit tools out of .claude/, so you make the copy yourself, but they do not cover .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. On macOS or Linux you can link the folders instead of copying them: see Going further.



Activity 2: Write a skill and test it


A house figure style (15 minutes)


Goal: write a skill and grade a figure made with it against your instructor’s baseline made without it, so that you judge the skill by what it changes, not by its own report.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean (your AGENTS.md committed), Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. The baseline, made without the skill. Your instructor runs this prompt on screen and shows the figure Claude Code makes. You don’t run it: it only needs making once, and before the skill exists.
Prompt (Claude Code, run by your instructor):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md") creates and opens the file. Paste in:
---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.
Copy it into .claude/skills/ with the fs::dir_copy() line above (you do this yourself, because .claude/ is protected from the agent). Type /skills: house-figures should be listed, with no restart (if it is not, type /reload-skills).
3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
Read the edit before you approve it. If it asks to run the script, choose No: you run it yourself in the next step.
4. Grade it. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so the script has to run on its own, then run source(here::here("scripts", "fig_house.R")) and open the figure it saved in outputs/. For three rules you can see at a glance, compare your figure with your instructor’s baseline:


Rule
Baseline (no skill)
Your figure (with skill)



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




5. n per group shown





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as Block 3, with today’s date, naming the skill you tested and what you kept or changed in its output. Commit it with the skill (both folders) and scripts/fig_house.R.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists and its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. If no figure appears in outputs/, ask the agent to save it there with ggsave(), as AGENTS.md asks. Out of time? Commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked, then switch to checkpoint-skills.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?






TipStretch: test the trigger





In a new conversation (/clear), test the trigger: “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill; “Make a figure of metabolic_rate_post by treatment_arm for a poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, what makes the output trustworthy is the grading in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once for every conversation, and package a procedure as a skill you invoke by name, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed; grade the output and run the figure code.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules (renv, fresh R session, seeds); Blocks 7 and 8 check the agent kept to them.

Record: add a line to docs/ai-log.md naming the skill you tested and what you changed in its output.

# Publication figures

This skill governs production of figures that will be seen by an external audience. It is self-contained: the house rules below apply even if the project has no instruction file.

## House rules

- Tidyverse style, native pipe `|>`, `here::here()` for every path.
- British spelling in titles, labels, legends and comments.
- Never produce pie charts, dual y-axes, 3D effects, or bar charts with error bars ("dynamite plots") when the raw data exist.

## Missing information

If information you need is missing (the audience, a variable's unit, the fitted model), ask the user once, in a single message, before writing code. If the user tells you to proceed without it, or you are working unattended (for example as a cloud agent on a pull request), choose the safe default this skill gives, record the choice in a code comment and, if there is one, in the pull request description, and continue.

## Project toolkit

The packages this skill uses are listed below. Check that each one you need is
in `renv.lock`; if one is missing, stop and ask before installing anything:

- `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `here`, `scales` for core plotting, composition, paths, and label formatting.
- `ggdist` for raincloud and half-eye distributions: `stat_halfeye()`, `stat_pointinterval()`.
- `ggbeeswarm` for moderate-n group displays: `geom_quasirandom()`.
- `colorspace` for palettes: `scale_*_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2")`, `scale_*_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis")`, `scale_*_continuous_diverging(palette = "Blue-Red")`, and the HCL generators (`sequential_hcl()`, `diverging_hcl()`) used by the brand-seeded scales in `theme-project.R`.
- `emmeans` for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts: `emmeans(model, specs = "var")`, `pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")`.
- `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` as the rendering layer for emmeans-derived contrasts. Never `ggpubr::stat_compare_means()`, which performs unadjusted pairwise t-tests by default.
- `ggh4x` for nested or hierarchical faceting: `facet_nested()`, `facet_nested_wrap()`, `guide_axis_nested()`.
- `ragg` for raster output via `ggsave(device = ragg::agg_png)`.
- `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` for the colour-vision-deficiency check.
- `showtext` (optional) for the project font; without it `theme_project()` falls back to the device's default font.

Do not introduce additional plotting packages without amending this list. Do not reach for `cowplot` themes when `theme_minimal()` or `theme_project()` will do. Do not hand-write manual hex colour vectors as data scales: use the `colorspace` palettes or the brand-seeded constructors in `theme-project.R`, both of which keep palettes CVD-checkable. A single fixed colour for a single-group or highlight geom is permitted and is not a "data scale".

## Colour

The colour-vision-deficiency check (`cvdPlot()`, below) is the final arbiter: a palette that fails it must be replaced, regardless of brand intent.

**No brand specified (default).** Use `colorspace::scale_*` functions, matched to data structure.

**Brand specified.** When the request names a brand colour (for example, "use a brand colour of darkblue"), call `set_brand("darkblue")` once after sourcing `theme-project.R`. `set_brand()` accepts any R colour name or hex string. The brand colour then seeds:

- single-colour and highlight geoms, via `brand_base()`;
- sequential continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_seq()`;
- the **high** arm of diverging continuous scales: `scale_*_brand_div(midpoint = <value>)`. The low arm is the brand's complementary hue, so the two arms always contrast, unless you name a second brand colour with `set_brand(<brand>, div_low = <colour>)`.

**Categorical colour is never brand-seeded.** One seed colour cannot generate a coherent, CVD-safe set of distinct hues. For unordered groups, use `colorspace` "Dark 2"; `scale_*_brand_qual()` in `theme-project.R` is the same palette and takes no `base` or `n` argument. The brand colour can still mark one focal group, with the other groups in grey.

| Data structure | Palette type | colorspace default | With a brand set |
|----------------|--------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Discrete, unordered groups | Qualitative | `Dark 2` | `Dark 2` (`scale_*_brand_qual()` is identical) |
| Discrete, ordered groups | Sequential discrete | `Purples 3` | `Purples 3` (the brand scales are continuous only) |
| Continuous, one-directional | Sequential | `Viridis` | `scale_*_brand_seq()` |
| Continuous, midpoint-centred | Diverging | `Blue-Red` | `scale_*_brand_div()` |

If a brand-seeded scale fails the CVD check, replace it with the colorspace default in the same row and record the fallback in a comment.

Categorical groupings must use redundant encoding: shape for points, linetype for lines. Colour alone is not sufficient.

## Statistical annotations workflow

Pairwise contrasts come from `emmeans::emmeans()` and `emmeans::pairs()` with an explicit adjustment method (`tukey`, `holm`, or similar). Render brackets with `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()`, supplying a data frame of contrasts.

Filter to significant contrasts before drawing. Format p-values with `scales::label_pvalue()` so very small values appear as `<0.001` rather than `0.000`.

A worked example is in `emmeans-bridge.R`.

## Error bars

Three options, not interchangeable:

- **Standard deviation:** spread of individual observations. Use when describing population variability.
- **Standard error of the mean:** precision of the sample mean. Shrinks with sample size.
- **95% confidence interval:** the recommended default. Prefer model-based intervals via `emmeans` where a model exists, otherwise from `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal)`.

The choice must appear in the y axis label.

## Multiple panels and shared legends

When composing panels with `patchwork` and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")`, collection merges only guides that are identical in aesthetic, scale, breaks, and title (`name`). It deduplicates by guide specification, not by visual appearance, and it never removes a guide it judges different. Two failures follow: panels that encode the same variable through different aesthetics (`fill` in one, `colour` plus `shape` in another) or different palettes produce one legend each; and a panel encoding a genuinely different variable produces its own legend, which is correct.

Resolve the layout from the plot specifications:

- **Same variable, same palette, across all panels:** produce one shared legend. Designate the panel with the richest encoding (e.g. colour plus shape) as the legend-bearer, because that legend is a complete key for the simpler panels but not the reverse. Apply the identical scale call and an identical `name` in every panel, then suppress the guide on every non-bearing panel with `guides(<aesthetic> = "none")`. Record the choice of bearer in a comment.
- **Panels encode different variables:** do not force collection into one key. Keep the separate legends; merging them would mislabel a panel.

A mismatched `name`, a differing aesthetic or scale, or a missing suppression line will silently leave more than one legend for the same variable. After composing, confirm exactly one legend appears per distinct variable. A worked skeleton is in `patchwork-template.R`.

## Saving

Always save to `outputs/figures/` via `here::here()` in both PDF and PNG formats. Specify `width`, `height`, `units`, and `dpi` explicitly; do not rely on `ggsave()` defaults. Use `ragg::agg_png` as the device for PNG output with `bg = "white"`. PDF uses the default device.

The agent cannot verify visual accessibility. Insert this line at the end of the script and flag it for the investigator to run and inspect:

# ==============================================================================
# Project theme and palette construction for ggplot2.
#
# Colour policy (authoritative; see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * No brand set         -> use colorspace palettes directly.
#   * Brand set            -> set_brand("darkblue") sets the base colour (used by
#                             single-colour and highlight geoms) and reseeds the
#                             sequential ramp and the diverging HIGH arm. The
#                             low arm becomes the brand's complementary hue
#                             unless set_brand() is given div_low. Sequential
#                             and diverging are
#                             generated via colorspace HCL generators
#                             (CVD-robust, monotonic luminance).
#   * Categorical colour is NEVER brand-seeded: scale_*_brand_qual() delegate to
#                             colorspace "Dark 2", which sizes itself to the data.
#                             A single seed cannot make a coherent multi-hue set.
#   * Single-group / highlight geoms default to brand_base(), teal until reset.
#
# Manual hex palettes are NOT used as data scales. Only the base colour is used
# directly, and only for single-colour or highlight geoms.
#
# theme_project() here is the full version of the simple theme_project() taught
# in the ggplot chapter (Block 3: Themes and scales). It keeps the same name and
# base_size argument, and adds a font, furniture colours and axis_type.
#
# Dependencies: ggplot2 (>= 3.5), colorspace, scales; showtext + sysfonts for
#   fonts (optional: without them the device's default font is used);
#   colorBlindness for the accessibility check.
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)

# ---- Brand state and setter --------------------------------------------------
# A single mutable brand state lets one call rebrand everything downstream.
# `set_brand("darkblue")` sets the base colour, which seeds the sequential ramp
# and the diverging high arm. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.

.brand_state <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"  # teal default
.brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"  # navy default for the diverging low arm

#' Normalise a colour name or hex to a hex string
#' @keywords internal
.as_hex <- function(col) {
  rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(col)  # accepts R colour names and hex
  grDevices::rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

#' Set the project brand colour
#'
#' Sets the base colour used by single-colour and highlight geoms, the
#' sequential ramp and the diverging high arm. Call once at the top of a
#' script: `set_brand("darkblue")`. Accepts any R colour name or hex string.
#'
#' @param base Brand colour (name or hex).
#' @param div_low Optional colour for the diverging low arm. If `NULL` (the
#'   default), the low arm uses the hue opposite the brand colour on the HCL
#'   colour wheel, so the two arms always contrast.
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
set_brand <- function(base, div_low = NULL) {
  .brand_state$base <- .as_hex(base)
  .brand_state$div_low <- if (is.null(div_low)) {
    .complement_of(.brand_state$base)
  } else {
    .as_hex(div_low)
  }
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Colour with the opposite HCL hue, for the diverging low arm
#' @keywords internal
.complement_of <- function(col) {
  hue <- (.hue_of(col) + 180) %% 360
  colorspace::hex(colorspace::polarLUV(L = 40, C = 60, H = hue), fixup = TRUE)
}

#' Reset the brand to the teal/navy default
#' @return Invisibly, the resolved brand state as a list.
#' @export
reset_brand <- function() {
  .brand_state$base    <- "#09baba"
  .brand_state$div_low <- "#2c4977"
  invisible(as.list(.brand_state))
}

#' Current brand base colour
#'
#' Returns the current brand base as a hex string. It is a function, not a value,
#' so it reflects the most recent `set_brand()` call. Use as `brand_base()`.
#' @return A hex colour string.
#' @export
brand_base <- function() .brand_state$base

# ---- Internal: font registration ---------------------------------------------

# Returns TRUE if `family` is available to showtext, FALSE otherwise, so the
# theme can fall back to the device's default font rather than warn on every
# text element.
.register_project_font <- function(family = "Open Sans") {
  if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) {
    return(FALSE)
  }
  showtext::showtext_auto(enable = TRUE)
  if (!(family %in% sysfonts::font_families())) {
    try(sysfonts::font_add_google(family, family), silent = TRUE)
  }
  family %in% sysfonts::font_families()
}

#' Project theme
#'
#' A composable ggplot2 theme controlling non-data aesthetics only. It sets no
#' data-encoding colours; pair it with a scale constructor (see below). Furniture
#' colours (title, axis labels, gridlines) are decorative and need not be
#' CVD-safe; the strip background is deliberately neutral grey so it is not
#' mistaken for a data signal when a fill palette is present. Furniture colours do
#' not track the brand by design; rebrand them by editing the literals below.
#'
#' @param base_size Base font size in points. Default 12 (journal/lab-report
#'   floor; raise to 14-20 for poster, talk, or public-engagement).
#' @param base_family Base font family. Default "Open Sans".
#' @param base_line_size Base line size. Default 0.5.
#' @param base_rect_size Base rectangle size. Default 0.5.
#' @param axis_type "categorical" or "continuous"; controls gridlines.
#' @return A ggplot2 theme object.
#' @export
theme_project <- function(base_size = 12,
                          base_family = "Open Sans",
                          base_line_size = 0.5,
                          base_rect_size = 0.5,
                          axis_type = c("categorical", "continuous")) {

  axis_type <- match.arg(axis_type)
  if (!.register_project_font(base_family)) {
    base_family <- ""  # device default font
  }

  title_col <- "#2c4977"  # decorative furniture only
  label_col <- "#41566f"
  muted_col <- "#5d6b7d"

  base <- ggplot2::theme(
    line = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#000000", linewidth = base_line_size),
    rect = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", colour = "#000000",
                                 linewidth = base_rect_size),
    text = ggplot2::element_text(family = base_family, colour = "#000000",
                                 size = base_size),
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0,
                                       size = ggplot2::rel(1.4),
                                       margin = ggplot2::margin(8, 0, 6, 0),
                                       colour = title_col),
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, size = ggplot2::rel(1.1),
                                          margin = ggplot2::margin(2, 0, 0, 0),
                                          colour = label_col),
    plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, size = ggplot2::rel(0.8),
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(6, 0, 0, 0),
                                         colour = muted_col),
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 4, 0, 0)),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = muted_col, size = ggplot2::rel(0.9)),
    axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(colour = label_col,
                                         margin = ggplot2::margin(4, 0, 0, 0)),
    panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#e9e9e9", colour = NA),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#2c4977",

    panel.border = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = base_line_size, colour = "black"),

    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col)
    )
  } else {
    grid_theme <- ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = grid_col),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank()
    )
  }

  base + grid_theme
}

# ---- Brand-seeded palette constructors ---------------------------------------
# These wrap colorspace HCL generators, seeded on the current brand colour, so
# the ramp is perceptually based with monotonic luminance. With no set_brand()
# call the seed is teal; callers may also pass `base`/`low`/`high` explicitly,
# which always overrides the brand state. If no brand is intended at all, use
# colorspace::scale_*_{qualitative,sequential,diverging} directly.

#' Hue (HCL) of a colour, for seeding colorspace generators
#' @keywords internal
.hue_of <- function(col) {
  hcl <- colorspace::coords(as(colorspace::hex2RGB(.as_hex(col)), "polarLUV"))
  unname(hcl[, "H"])
}

#' Brand-seeded sequential scale (colour)
#'
#' Single-hue sequential ramp seeded on `base`, generated in HCL so luminance is
#' monotonic. Light-to-dark by default.
#'
#' @param base Seed colour. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops. Default 7.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_seq
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_seq <- function(base = brand_base(), n = 7, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::sequential_hcl(
    n = n, h = .hue_of(base), c = c(70, 10), l = c(25, 95), power = 1.2,
    rev = TRUE
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, ...)
}

#' Brand-seeded diverging scale (colour)
#'
#' Two-hue diverging ramp seeded on `low` and `high`, generated in HCL with a
#' balanced neutral midpoint. Supply `midpoint` to centre on a meaningful value.
#'
#' @param low Seed colour for the low arm. Defaults to navy or, after
#'   `set_brand()`, to the brand's complementary hue (or its `div_low`).
#' @param high Seed colour for the high arm. Defaults to the current `brand_base()`.
#' @param midpoint Data value mapped to the neutral midpoint. Default 0.
#' @param n Number of interpolation stops (odd recommended). Default 11.
#' @param ... Passed to `ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                    high = brand_base(),
                                    midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_colour_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_div
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_div <- function(low = .brand_state$div_low,
                                  high = brand_base(),
                                  midpoint = 0, n = 11, ...) {
  cols <- colorspace::diverging_hcl(
    n = n, h = c(.hue_of(low), .hue_of(high)),
    c = 80, l = c(35, 95), power = 1.0
  )
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = cols, rescaler = ~ scales::rescale_mid(.x, mid = midpoint), ...
  )
}

#' Qualitative scale (colour) for categorical groups
#'
#' Categorical palettes are NOT brand-seeded. A single brand colour cannot
#' generate a coherent, CVD-safe multi-hue set: spreading hues from one anchor
#' discards the seed's own chroma and luminance and walks through arbitrary
#' intermediate hues. This constructor therefore delegates to `colorspace`'s
#' `Dark 2` qualitative palette, which is built for mutual distinctness and is
#' CVD-tested, and which sizes itself to the number of groups (so it cannot raise
#' "Insufficient values in manual scale"). Reserve the brand colour for the
#' sequential ramp, the diverging high arm, and single-colour or highlight geoms,
#' where one seed genuinely works. Always pair with a redundant aesthetic (shape
#' or linetype).
#'
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @return A ggplot2 scale.
#' @export
scale_colour_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

#' @rdname scale_colour_brand_qual
#' @param ... Passed to `colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative()`.
#' @export
scale_fill_brand_qual <- function(...) {
  colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", ...)
}

# ---- Example usage -----------------------------------------------------------
# Set a brand once, then everything downstream follows:
#   set_brand("darkblue")
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_seq()          # darkblue-seeded sequential
#   ... + geom_point(colour = brand_base())# darkblue single-colour geom
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_div(midpoint = 0) # complementary low arm, darkblue high
#
# No brand (default path): colorspace directly.
#   ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = g, shape = g)) + geom_point() +
#     colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2") +
#     theme_project(axis_type = "continuous")
#
# Per-call override (ignores brand state):
#   ... + scale_fill_brand_seq(base = "#2c4977")
#
# Accessibility check is mandatory; a brand-seeded palette that fails it falls
# back to its colorspace default (Viridis for sequential, Blue-Red for diverging):
#   colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig1)

# emmeans-bridge.R
# Worked emmeans-to-ggpubr annotation pattern.
# Requires a fitted model object: fitted by code in this project that you have
# run or can read, or present in the user's live R session where your tool can
# see it. Never fabricate test statistics from descriptive data.

library(emmeans)
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# model <- lm(value ~ group, data = data)  # supplied upstream

# fig1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) + geom_boxplot()   # supplied upstream
#
# ADAPT: `fig1` is your existing ggplot. `panel_yrange()` reads layer 1 by
# default, which must be the geom whose data the brackets sit above (e.g. the
# boxplot). If layer 1 is a reference line or similar, pass the correct index,
# e.g. panel_yrange(fig1, layer = 2L).

emm <- emmeans::emmeans(model, specs = "group")

# lowest and highest y values drawn by one layer ----
panel_yrange <- function(p, layer = 1L) {
  d <- ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[layer]]
  # positional y columns ggplot may compute
  cols <- intersect(
    c("ymin_final", "ymin", "lower", "ymax_final", "ymax", "upper", "y"),
    names(d)
  )
  if (length(cols) == 0L) {
    stop("No y-position column found in layer ", layer, ".")
  }
  range(unlist(d[cols]), na.rm = TRUE)
}

y_range <- panel_yrange(fig1)
# step between brackets as a fraction of the data range, so positions work for
# negative values and for data far from zero
y_step <- 0.07 * diff(y_range)

contrasts_df <-
  pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    contrast, delim = " - ", names = c("group1", "group2")
  ) |>
  # emmeans wraps level names containing spaces or operators in parentheses
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(
    c(group1, group2), \(x) stringr::str_remove_all(x, "^\\(|\\)$")
  )) |>
  dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    p.label = scales::label_pvalue()(p.value),
    y.position = y_range[2] + y_step * dplyr::row_number()
  )

# headroom so the top bracket isn't clipped: highest position + one more step
y_top <- y_range[2] + y_step * (nrow(contrasts_df) + 1)

fig1 +
  stat_pvalue_manual(
    contrasts_df, label = "p.label", tip.length = 0.01
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(NA, y_top))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Composite figure: panels sharing ONE collected legend.
#
# Precondition: every panel maps the SAME grouping variable to the SAME palette.
# If a panel encodes a different variable, do not use this pattern for it; give it
# its own scale and accept a separate legend (forcing one key would mislabel it).
#
# Colour policy (see pub-figures SKILL.md):
#   * The shared grouping variable is categorical, so every panel uses
#     colorspace qualitative "Dark 2", with or without a brand. Categorical
#     colour is never brand-seeded. Keep an identical `name` across panels so
#     the legend collects to one.
#
# Legend-bearer: chosen here by richness of encoding. If unclear, use the panel
# with the most aesthetics mapped to the group and record the choice.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Legend-bearing panel: richest encoding (colour + shape), legend retained.
# Redundant encoding (shape) is required by the skill, and conveniently makes this
# panel a complete key for the simpler ones.
p_keep <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = y1, colour = group_var, shape = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15), name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X1", y = "Y1") 

# Other panels: identical palette and identical name, guide suppressed.
# Suppression is what collection cannot do for you. Repeat per additional panel.
p_other <- data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x2, y = y2, colour = group_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 2", name = "Group") +
  labs(x = "X2", y = "Y2") +
  guides(colour = "none")

# Letters refer to plots in the order added (A = p_keep, B = p_other).
layout <- "
AB
"

fig1 <- p_keep + p_other +
  patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

Glossary




term
definition



canary
A fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed.


front matter
The block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill's name and description, or a Quarto document's options.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


skill
A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.


symbolic link
A file-system entry that points to another folder or file, so one copy can appear in two places. On Windows, copying the folder is usually simpler.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Exercise 2: Deny rules


Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)


Goal: see a deny ruleA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. refuse, add one of your own and find the route the rules do not cover, so that you know what your repository prevents and what only git detects.
Start state: Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Work on a scratch file, never on real data.
1. Make a scratch file and read the rules. In the R console:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Commit it in the Git pane, so git can show any later change to it. In Claude Code, type /permissions: the 17 deny rules your repository ships are listed.
2. See a rule refuse.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
“Denied by a permission rule” means the rule held, whatever the model intended. If the model declines by itself, citing AGENTS.md, that was a request that happened to work: reply “This is a scratch file; please make the edit with your edit tool” to see the rule refuse.
Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. If Claude Code asks to write the file another way, answer No: step 4 tries that.
3. Add a rule yourself. In /permissions, add Read(/data/confidential/**), one of the confidential-data habits from Block 3. When asked where to save it, choose the project’s shared settings file, .claude/settings.json, not the local one (see How it works). It applies at once.
4. Find the gap.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can: it writes to a scratch file, and you want to see what catches the change. Approve it. The Git pane now shows the file as modified, and Diff shows the new line: git caught what no rule prevented.
5. Tidy up. Revert the file in the Git pane, then delete it, so no scratch file is left among the raw data:

file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

6. Record, test and commit. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, in the same form as before, noting which requests were refused and what git caught. Then restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

test_controls.R checks that Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in place and that no command is approved in advance; test_ai_log.R checks your new line. Commit the deletion of scratch.csv, your rule in .claude/settings.json and the log line together.
You are done when you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen the Git pane catch the R write, scratch.csv is gone, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your rule and log line are committed.
If it goes wrong: if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If “no command is approved in advance” fails, you chose don’t ask again: remove that allow rule in /permissions.






NoteAt the command line





git add/git commit for step 1, git diff data/raw for step 4, git restore then git rm data/raw/scratch.csv for step 5, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')" then git add/git commit for step 6. See checking work.
