With no hook registered, only the approval prompt stands between R code and the file. Prevent where you can, detect everywhere. And test every control: one you have not seen refuse something is one you are assuming.











NoteHow it works: where the rules live





Your repository’s .claude/settings.json starts the project in Manual mode ("defaultMode": "default": asks before every edit and command) and holds 17 deny rules protecting the raw data, the data provider’s note, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfile and the settings themselves. You never need to edit it: /permissions shows the rules and adds new ones.


{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / anchors a pattern to the project root. Edit rules cover Claude Code’s file-editing tools and shell output redirects (> file), not R code it runs, and the documentation does not say they cover rm, mv or cp. The rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 8. Edit(/renv.lock) keeps renv::status() a real check.
Why the shared settings file. /permissions can save a rule to .claude/settings.json, which is committed with the project, or to the local .claude/settings.local.json, which git ignores. Only a rule in the shared file reaches a commit, and so everyone who clones the repository. Answering don’t ask again saves an allow rule, usually in the local file, which is why test_controls.R checks that no command is approved in advance.









TipUsing another tool





The exercises use Claude Code. Posit Assistant sets permissions per tool in .posit/assistant/settings.json (for example "bash": {"rm *": "deny"}); deny rules hold in every mode, including auto and YOLO. It has no documented path rules for file edits, so rely on the Git pane in step 4 of Exercise 2. It blocks reading .env and .Renviron by default.









TipInstructor: demonstration of a guard hook





A hookA command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it. is a command that Claude Code itself (the harness, not the model) runs before every tool callA single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls., so it does not depend on the model following a request. Your instructor saves the guard hook from Going further as hooks/guard_protected_paths.R (the template does not ship hooks/), registers it, and repeats step 4: the hook, written in R, blocks any call mentioning data/raw, so it blocks this one before any approval prompt. Then the same write using here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"): the text data/raw never appears, so the hook lets it through. A text-matching hook is a tripwire, not a wall; the Git pane still shows the change. The GitHub review gate (CODEOWNERSA GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review., branch protectionGitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.) is in Going further.









NoteSet up controls in your own project





Your workshop repository came with its controls. A new project of your own starts with none, so set them up before the agent’s first task:


Git first. In the R console, usethis::use_git(), and make a first commit.

Add a starter settings.json. Download the one below, save it as .claude/settings.json, and edit the paths to match your project. It starts in Manual mode and protects raw data, test references, the lockfile, credentials and itself. Add project-specific rules with /permissions.

Ask for git checks. Copy the Version control section of your workshop AGENTS.md into your project’s instruction file.

Test it. Ask the agent to edit a protected file and watch the rule refuse; copy tests/test_controls.R and change its list of rules to yours. Then commit.



 Download the starter settings.json








TipReference: the starter settings.json







{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}





Let Claude draft rules, never decide them. You can ask it to propose deny rules for a project, but read each one: a rule with a wrong path, such as a missing leading /, protects nothing and fails silently. Claude Code asks before every write to .claude/, and the starter file’s Edit(/.claude/**) refuses such writes outright, so you install the rules yourself.
Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in /permissions. For confidential data, add the five habits in Block 3; and since settings and hooks are code, trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw data, references and checks are protected, trusted because you have seen a deny rule refuse, seen git catch the route it misses, and have a test that fails if the rules are weakened.

Check: watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does not cover. What gets past the rules shows in the Git pane, Block 7’s checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. test or test_controls.R.

Reproduce: the rules live in .claude/settings.json, committed with the project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection.

Record: your log line from step 6 notes which requests were refused and what git caught.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipA guard hook





Claude Code itself, the harness rather than the model, runs a PreToolUse hook before each tool call and passes it the pending call as JSON on standard input (stdin). If the hook exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is passed to the model. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for this, so one script can serve both.
The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code that mentions a protected path.

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)

The template does not ship hooks/: save the script yourself as hooks/guard_protected_paths.R, for example with usethis::edit_file("hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"). It runs with Rscript --vanilla, so it does not start renv, and jsonlite must be installed in your user library.
Register it with Claude Code by adding a hooks key to .claude/settings.json, alongside the existing permissions key. The deny rules protect .claude/, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
The matcher lists the tool names the hook runs for.
Register it with Posit Assistant in .posit/assistant/settings.json. The tool names differ: edit, bash, and executeR for R code run in your session.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.


Test the hook before you trust it


Goal: check the guard denies a protected path and allows a harmless call, so that you know it works before you rely on it.
Hooks fail open. If the script crashes, for example because jsonlite is not installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call. So test the script directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude Code does, a fresh Rscript --vanilla process given the tool call on standard input, and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In the R console:

rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R"))

run_hook <- function(json) {
  system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json,
          stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
}

# can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes
system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")),
        stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)

# a call naming a protected path: expect 2
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}')

# a harmless call: expect 0
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}')

Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook is broken and is silently allowing everything.
Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions data/raw, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.
To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, temporarily add a PostToolUse hook with no matcher that appends its input to a log file (Posit Assistant’s hooks documentation gives an example), and read the log.
You are done when the protected call returns 2, the harmless call returns 0, and the request from step 4 of Exercise 2 is denied before you see an approval prompt.











TipBreak your own guard







Red-team the tripwire


Goal: get a write past the guard hook, so that you see where a text-matching guard stops.
The live block removed the scratch file at the end. Recreate it first, in the R console, and commit it from the Git pane:

writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))

Prompt (Claude Code):
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
The guard searches for the text data/raw. This call never contains it, because here::here() assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.
This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code’s documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall. The Git pane still shows the change. Revert the file there, then delete it and commit the deletion, as in steps 5 and 6 of Exercise 2.
You are done when the here::here() write has got past the guard, the Git pane has shown the change, and you have deleted scratch.csv again.


Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed. What happens when the agent tries to edit a protected file?

The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve itThe edit goes ahead: hooks fail open, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the callThe agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installedThe edit is blocked only in plan mode










TipThe review gate on GitHub





Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely, such as the Copilot cloud agent. There, the controls are on the repository itself. Neither file below is in the workshop template; you create them.
1. CODEOWNERS. Create .github/CODEOWNERS on your default branch:
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/hooks/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
/.posit/              @your-github-username
Code owners are requested for review automatically when a pull request changes the files they own. CODEOWNERS works in public repositories on free plans; for private repositories it requires a paid plan.
2. Branch protection. In the repository settings, add a rule for main that requires a pull request before merging, requires review from code owners, and requires the r-checks status check to pass. The r-checks workflow is set up in the Going further section of Block 8.
3. Test it. Open a pull request that changes a file under tests/, for example by asking the Copilot cloud agent to “update the test to use a tolerance of 1e-6”. Confirm that the pull request cannot merge until you have reviewed it.
GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request. In a repository where you are the only person, a pull request you open yourself may need an administrator override, which is a reason to test this gate with an agent’s pull request.









TipFeedback hooks: useful, with a warning





Hooks can do more than block. A PostToolUse hook can run lintr on each R file the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A Stop hook can run the test suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is powerful and dangerous: an agent told it cannot stop until tests pass may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect tests/.

title: Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection
text:
Glossary




term
definition



branch protection
GitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.


checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


CODEOWNERS
A GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


hook
A command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it.


instruction file
A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.


tool call
A single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.

title: Block 6: Build your own agent in R
text:
Before you start


ellmer talks to Claude and runs the loop. Your repository’s renv.lock pins it, so renv::restore() installed it. Never run install.packages() inside the project.

Your API key comes from an Anthropic Console account, which is separate from a Claude Pro or Max subscription. Setting up Claude Code saved it in your user-level .Renviron as AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY: outside every repository, never in a script, and named so that Claude Code never offers to bill it.

Every request costs money. chat$get_cost() shows what a conversation has cost so far. The code names its model, claude-sonnet-5-5, so your AI-use log can record it; swapping in claude-opus-5-5 gives the most capable model at a higher cost per request.

title: Block 6: Build your own agent in R
text:
Talk to a model, then give it a tool (8 minutes)


Goal: see what one request to a model is, and what a tool request is, so that nothing your agent does in Task 2 is a surprise.
1. Have a conversation. In the R console:

library(ellmer)

key <- function() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat

Printing chat shows the conversation as turnsOne message in a conversation with a model: either yours (the user turn) or the model’s reply (the assistant turn). Tool results go back to the model inside a user turn.. The second question works only because ellmer sends the whole conversation so far with each request: the model keeps nothing between requests. That is the context window from Block 1, and why a long conversation costs more per question.
2. Give it a tool. A tool is an R function the model may ask you to run:

today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days until 25 December?")
chat

The model sees only the tool’s name and description. Its first reply is a request, “call today”; ellmer runs today() on your computer and sends the result back; then the model answers. That is two requestsOne call to the model, with the whole conversation so far, and its reply. A single question can take several requests when the model asks for tools before it answers. for one question.
You are done when you can point, in the printed chat, to the tool request and to the tool result, and say which of them ran on your computer.
If it goes wrong: if the first chat$chat() reports a missing or invalid key, check Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY") != "", and restart R after editing .Renviron.

text:
Task 2: run your agent


Run your agent (20 minutes)


Goal: watch your own agent write, test and fix a translation while you approve every write and run, so that you see exactly where Manual mode and a deny rule act.
Start state: main, Git pane clean, R’s working directory at the repository’s root (as it is when you open the project).
1. Load the agent. Nothing is sent to the model yet:

source(here::here("agent", "mini_agent.R"))

2. Give it the task. The original base R code is legacy_rate_summary() in tests/test_translation.R, which also checks the translation:

chat$chat(paste(
  "Write a function summarise_rate_tidy(data) in scripts/functions/summaries.R",
  "whose output matches legacy_rate_summary() in tests/test_translation.R.",
  "Use dplyr and the native pipe; it must work in a fresh R session.",
  "Write only that file, and no tests. Then run",
  "testthat::test_file('tests/test_translation.R') with run_r, and fix the",
  "function until the test passes."
))

3. Decide each request. Reads run without asking. For a write_file or run_r request, read what it prints and choose Yes only for a write to scripts/functions/summaries.R or a run of the test. Refuse the first test run on purpose: the agent stops and explains. Then let it continue:

chat$chat("Go ahead and run the test.")

4. Look inside.

chat               # every turn: your prompt, its tool requests, the results
count_requests()   # how many requests it sent to the model
chat$get_tokens()  # the tokens it sent and received

5. Check its work yourself. The agent’s “the test passes” is a claim. Read the diff of scripts/functions/summaries.R in the Git pane, then restart R (Session → Restart R) and run:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

6. Record and commit. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md with today’s date, for example 2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-sonnet-5-5); translated the rate summary to tidyverse; kept after reading the diff and running the tests, then commit summaries.R and the log.


Did your agent notice the missing value?

aggregate() with a formula silently drops the animal whose metabolic_rate_post is missing, so the original’s mean and count leave it out. A literal tidyverse translation keeps it: an NA mean and a count one too high. The test compares against the original, so the agent had to match that behaviour, and if it read the test it probably did so without comment. The test checks “the same as the original”, not “correct”: Block 8 returns to that difference.

You are done when test_translation.R passes in your own run, the Git pane showed only summaries.R and your log changed, you can say how many requests and tokens the task took, and both are committed.
If it goes wrong:


The agent loops or goes off course: answer No, then steer it with chat$chat("…"), or source() the file again to start a new conversation.

A refused path you expected to work: check getwd() is the repository’s root.

An unwanted change: Revert it in the Git pane.







TipWhat did it cost?





chat$get_cost() turns the tokens into money when ellmer knows the model’s price. If it shows NA, run ellmer::models_update_prices() once to refresh ellmer’s price list, or multiply the tokens from chat$get_tokens() by the prices on Anthropic’s pricing page. claude-opus-5-5, set at the top of mini_agent.R, is a larger model at a higher price per token.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 0: Check the safeguards are in place
Cleaning mistakes are silent: a missing-value code treated as a measurement, the same animal kept twice, a row quietly dropped. Here an agent writes and runs the whole cleaning script from one command, against a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI. you own, and one test run tells you whether to trust it.
⏱ ~55 minutes · Start on main (or checkpoint-skills), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Recipe check (3 minutes)


Goal: confirm the protections and the checks are in place before any cleaning starts, so that a mistake by the agent is blocked or caught rather than found later.
Start state: as at the top of the page; switch to checkpoint-skills, if you need it, in the Git pane’s branch menu.
1. The protections. In Claude Code, type /permissions and find four deny rulesA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.: Edit(/data/raw/**), Read(/docs/data_note.md), Edit(/docs/codebook.csv) and Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R). They keep the agent’s edit tools off the raw data, your codebook and the tests, and stop it reading the provider’s note (Step 2 shows why).
2. The checks. In the Files pane, tests/ holds test_cleaning.R, written from the agreed codebook before any cleaning code existed, and fixtures/raw_checksum.txt, a checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. of the raw file. The raw-data checksum test runs from the start; the others skip until clean data exist.
You are done when you have seen the four rules and the two files.
If it goes wrong: if /permissions lists no rules, check you started claude from the workshop repository’s Terminal tab; if the files are missing, switch to checkpoint-skills.








NoteHow the pieces fit





The steps follow the safe vibe-coding recipe from Block 3. The cleaning and the checks both read the codebook but never each other, so a misunderstanding in one is caught by the other.



Facts first


data/raw/voles_raw.csv, pinned by a checksum


00_profile.R


docs/profile*.csv


drafts from the profile


Agent’s draft codebook


you correct against docs/data_note.md


docs/codebook.csv




Two branches that read the codebook, never each other




Skill writes and runs scripts/01_clean.R


writes


Clean data, cleaning log, exclusion log




Shipped: the tests in test_cleaning.R, written from the agreed codebook






Then compare


One test run: raw data unchanged, every row accounted for, every change logged truthfully, nothing over-cleaned, every agreed rule obeyed, the same answer every time



Independence is the point: one misunderstanding cannot pass both branches.











TipBackground: why not simply ask a chatbot to clean the data?





In a 2025 study, language models given polluted tables missed codes such as -1 (a sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.) and rarely spotted near duplicates (Spreafico et al., 2025). Those error classes are planted here.

title: Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI
text:
Step 1: Profile the raw data


Profile (5 minutes)


Goal: count what is in the raw file with R rather than the model, so that the codebook draft in Step 2 starts from exact counts, not a model’s impression.
In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "00_profile.R"))
View(readr::read_csv(here::here("docs", "profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE))

The shipped script reads every column as text, so 9999 and -1 appear exactly as entered, and writes three tables to docs/: profile.csv (per column: missing values, distinct values, numeric minimum and maximum), profile_labels.csv (how often each spelling of sex and treatment_arm occurs) and profile_ids.csv (repeated IDs, and IDs of unusual length). Look for numbers far outside the rest, labels that differ only in spelling or case, and every ID in profile_ids.csv.
You are done when the three profile files exist in docs/ and you have noted anything that looks odd.
If it goes wrong: restart R (Session → Restart R) and run the lines again.








NoteThe shipped scripts/00_profile.R






# scripts/00_profile.R ----
# Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made.
# Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear
# exactly as entered.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

raw_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ----
profile_df <- raw_df |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design
  mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)),
    min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = column
  )

# every distinct label in the categorical columns ----
labels_df <- raw_df |>
  select(sex, treatment_arm) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |>
  count(column, value, sort = TRUE)

# identifiers that appear more than once, or whose length differs from the
# usual one (a possible formatting slip) ----
usual_length <- as.integer(names(which.max(table(nchar(raw_df$subject_id)))))
ids_df <- raw_df |>
  count(subject_id) |>
  mutate(unusual_length = nchar(subject_id) != usual_length) |>
  filter(n > 1 | unusual_length)

# print in full, and save each table so it can be opened, pasted or diffed ----
print(profile_df, n = Inf, width = Inf)
print(labels_df, n = Inf, width = Inf)
print(ids_df, width = Inf)
write_csv(profile_df, here("docs", "profile.csv"))
write_csv(labels_df, here("docs", "profile_labels.csv"))
write_csv(ids_df, here("docs", "profile_ids.csv"))

text:
Step 2: Draft the codebook with the agent, then audit it
The codebook is Day 2’s data dictionary (README chapter) with rules code can read. Its facts come from docs/data_note.md, which stands in for the methods sheet or email you would get from whoever collected the data. The agent is denied reading it, so it drafts from the profile alone, like an analyst who never asked for the note: that gap is the point.


Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes)


Goal: a codebook you own, drafted by the agent, corrected by you against the data note and committed, so that every cleaning rule traces to a fact you can defend.
1. Ask for a draft. The source column shows which entries are the agent’s own assumptions, so you know where to look first.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft a codebook for the raw voles data from docs/profile.csv,
docs/profile_labels.csv and docs/profile_ids.csv only, with the columns
column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source. In the source
column, say for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your
assumption. Write it to scratch/codebook_draft.csv and no other file.
Claude Code asks before it writes the file. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Approve this write. If the agent asks whether to commit the profile files first, reply No, go ahead: you commit them in step 4.
Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. The read rule stops Claude Code’s own reads of the note, not R code that opens it, so refuse any code that would.
2. Make it yours. In the R console, copy the draft into place (git ignores scratch/) and open it:

fs::file_copy(here::here("scratch", "codebook_draft.csv"), here::here("docs", "codebook.csv"))
usethis::edit_file("docs/codebook.csv")

The agent is denied editing docs/codebook.csv: the codebook is yours. (Avoid Excel, which can silently change quoted fields.)
3. Audit the draft. Before you open docs/data_note.md, answer:

Did the draft list 9999 as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement?
Did it notice that -1 is a code?
Where did its min and max come from? A range read off the data includes its errors, so valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol.

4. Correct it against the note, and commit. Open docs/data_note.md (also shown below the task) and edit docs/codebook.csv until every line traces to the note or to a decision you can defend, and its source says which. Where the note gives no unit (metabolic rate), write <unit>, not a guess: a guessed unit is an invented fact. Save, then commit docs/codebook.csv and the three profile files together, so the cleaning starts from a recorded version of your rules and Step 3 starts with a clean Git pane.
You are done when the codebook and the three profile files are committed, and every rule traces to the note or to your own decision.
If it goes wrong: short of time? Paste the codebook below into docs/codebook.csv and commit it with the profile files; it is what most groups converge on.








NoteThe shipped docs/data_note.md (open after step 3 of the task)







# Data note: vole metabolism experiment

From the colony manager who collected the data. One row per animal.

- **subject_id**: `V` followed by three digits (for example `V007`). Each
  animal appears once.
- **sex**: `M` or `F`.
- **treatment_arm**: `Control`, `Low_dose` or `High_dose`.
- **mass_pre_g**, **mass_post_g**: body mass in grams, before and after
  treatment. Adults in this colony weigh between 15 and 60 g. We entered
  `9999` when an animal could not be weighed.
- **metabolic_rate_post**: metabolic rate after treatment, from the
  respirometer. Valid readings lie between 5 and 30. We entered `-1` when the
  respirometry run failed.











NoteWhy a CSV, not a table in the README?





Code reads it. 01_clean.R reads docs/codebook.csv every time it runs, so the rules are never copied into the script by hand, and the over-cleaning test reads its min, max and missing_codes columns. A Markdown table is for people; a CSV is for people and code.





A codebook you could converge on

column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source
subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note; padding is a decision
sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note; recodes are a decision
treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note; case-insensitive matching is a decision
mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note
mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note
metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,<unit>,data note; no unit given
The note states the ID pattern, that each animal appears once, the allowed labels, the ranges and the missing-value codes. Padding short IDs and mapping other spellings onto the allowed labels are your decisions, and the source column says so. The note gives no unit for metabolic rate, so <unit> stays until you find it out.

Step 3: Clean with one command
The shipped skill clean-with-codebook holds the procedure; your codebook holds the facts. It writes scripts/01_clean.R, the only new script in this block.


Plan, review, then execute (15 minutes)


Goal: the skill writes and runs scripts/01_clean.R from your codebook, after you have approved its plan, so that every change to the data is made by a script you can rerun and is logged against a codebook rule.
Start state: the codebook and profile files committed, Git pane clean.
1. Invoke the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv.
2. Review its plan. The skill shows its plan as a message and waits. Read it, then reply in Claude Code: Yes, go ahead, or say what to change. A wrong rule is cheapest to catch here, before any file is written. Check that:

every rule cites a codebook row;
out-of-range values are set to NA and queried, not “corrected”;
no file outside scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/ will be written;
duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged.

3. Read each request. Claude Code still asks before each write and each run: approve what the plan described, and nothing else. New files should appear in the Git pane only in scripts/ and data/derived/. The skill runs the script twice, then the tests, and reports the output.
You are done when data/derived/ contains voles_clean.csv, cleaning_log.csv and exclusion_log.csv, and the agent has reported the test output.
If it goes wrong: if it stalls, loops or writes elsewhere, press Ctrl+C, Revert in the Git pane, and switch to checkpoint-cleaning (a working 01_clean.R and its outputs).








NoteWhat the skill tells the agent (clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md)





The skill ships in .agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/, copied to .claude/skills/, and runs only when you invoke it by name.


---
name: clean-with-codebook
description: >-
  Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a
  human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when
  asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook.
  Not for exploratory analysis or modelling.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Clean data against a codebook

## Hard constraints
1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit
   column types.
2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges,
   missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state.
3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R,
   scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails,
   report it; never change a check to make it pass.
4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log
   with a reason.
5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log.
6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to
   NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report.
   Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error.
7. No imputation.
8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the
   codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm.
2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask.
3. Write scripts/01_clean.R. It reads docs/codebook.csv when it runs; do not
   copy rules into the script by hand. Run it in a fresh R session
   (Rscript scripts/01_clean.R), then run it a second time and confirm the
   outputs are identical.
4. Run every test: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')". Report the
   output verbatim, including skips.

## Outputs (exact columns)
- data/derived/voles_clean.csv: raw_row, then the codebook columns. raw_row
  is the 1-based row number in the raw file, not counting the header.
- data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id (as it appears in the
  raw file), reason.
- data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value,
  new_value, rule.
- rule is one of: missing_code, label_recode, id_format, out_of_range_query.

## Final report
Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps
in the codebook you found.











TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant. Invoke the skill with the same prompt in Normal mode, so it asks before each change; use /plan first if you want the plan without any edits.

text:
Step 4: One check, in a fresh R session
The agent says its tests pass: that is a claim. One command, in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., turns it into evidence.


Run the checks (6 minutes)


Goal: run the tests yourself in a fresh R session, then commit, so that the agent’s “tests pass” becomes evidence you have seen.
1. Run every test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so that nothing left in your session can make a test pass, then in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

2. Read the change and record it. In the Git pane, Diff scripts/01_clean.R for anything the plan did not mention. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed), then commit the script, its outputs and the log.
You are done when every cleaning test passes (other blocks’ tests may skip) and the work, with its AI-log line, is committed.
If it goes wrong: a failing test names the problem. Ask the agent to fix 01_clean.R, quoting the test; never the test itself (it is deny-protected). Short of time? Switch to checkpoint-cleaning.








NoteWhat each test proves, and where the tests come from











Test in test_cleaning.R

A pass proves



raw data are unchanged
The raw file still matches its checksum: nothing changed it, by any route


every raw row is in the clean data or the exclusion log
No row was dropped silently, and every exclusion has a reason


every log entry is truthful
Each logged old value is the raw value, and each new value is the one in the clean file


every changed cell appears in the log
No change went unrecorded


no more values set to NA than the codebook explains
Nothing was over-cleaned


cleaning is reproducible
A fresh run writes byte-identical files


clean data pass every rule in the agreed codebook
IDs, labels and ranges obey the agreed codebook (a missing value is allowed)



The last test uses the agreed codebook’s rules (Step 2); the over-cleaning test reads your own docs/codebook.csv. If your ranges differ from the agreed ones, the two can disagree.
The course team wrote tests/test_cleaning.R from the agreed codebook, before any cleaning code existed, so it checks what the cleaning should do, not what one script happens to do. The agent did not write it and cannot edit it: Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R) is one of the deny rules you checked in Step 0. In your own projects, write these tests yourself, from your codebook, before you ask an agent to clean.





The shipped tests/test_cleaning.R


# tests/test_cleaning.R ----
# Block 7: the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, every
# change is logged truthfully, nothing was over-cleaned, and the clean data
# pass every codebook rule. Written from the agreed codebook, before any
# cleaning code existed. Raw values are read as text, exactly as entered, so a
# logged old value can be compared character for character.
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)

read_chr <- function(...) {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here(...),
    col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
  )
}

to_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name)
}

same <- function(x, y) (is.na(x) & is.na(y)) | (!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y)

clean_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")

cleaning_inputs <- function() {
  raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") |>
    dplyr::mutate(raw_row = as.character(dplyr::row_number()))
  clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
  list(
    raw = raw_df,
    clean = clean_df,
    excluded = read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv"),
    log = read_chr("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
    raw_long = to_long(raw_df, "raw_value"),
    clean_long = to_long(clean_df, "clean_value")
  )
}

test_that("raw data are unchanged", {
  checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
  skip_if_not(file.exists(checksum_path), "Block 7 Step 0 not done yet")
  recorded <- readLines(checksum_path)
  current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv")))
  expect_identical(current, recorded)
})

test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()

  expect_equal(nrow(x$raw), nrow(x$clean) + nrow(x$excluded))
  expect_setequal(c(x$clean$raw_row, x$excluded$raw_row), x$raw$raw_row)
  expect_false(any(is.na(x$excluded$reason) | x$excluded$reason == ""))
})

test_that("every log entry is truthful: old value from raw, new value in clean", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  wrong_old <- x$log |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(old_value, raw_value))
  wrong_new <- x$log |>
    dplyr::inner_join(x$clean_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::filter(!same(new_value, clean_value))
  expect_equal(nrow(wrong_old), 0)
  expect_equal(nrow(wrong_new), 0)
})

test_that("every changed cell appears in the log", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  numeric_cols <- c("mass_pre_g", "mass_post_g", "metabolic_rate_post")
  changed <- x$clean_long |>
    dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      # numbers are compared as numbers, so 28.30 and 28.3 count as unchanged
      differs = dplyr::if_else(
        column %in% numeric_cols,
        !same(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(clean_value)),
              suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw_value))),
        !same(clean_value, raw_value)
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(differs)
  unlogged <- dplyr::anti_join(changed, x$log, by = c("raw_row", "column"))
  expect_equal(nrow(unlogged), 0)
})

test_that("no more values were set to NA than the codebook explains", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  x <- cleaning_inputs()
  codebook <- read_chr("docs", "codebook.csv")
  numeric_rules <- dplyr::filter(codebook, !is.na(min) | !is.na(max) | !is.na(missing_codes))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(numeric_rules))) {
    col <- numeric_rules$column[[i]]
    codes <- trimws(strsplit(dplyr::coalesce(numeric_rules$missing_codes[[i]], ""), ";")[[1]])
    lo <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$min[[i]])
    hi <- as.numeric(numeric_rules$max[[i]])

    kept_raw <- x$raw[[col]][match(x$clean$raw_row, x$raw$raw_row)]
    value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(kept_raw))
    explained <- !is.na(kept_raw) & (
      kept_raw %in% codes |
        (!is.na(lo) & !is.na(value) & value < lo) |
        (!is.na(hi) & !is.na(value) & value > hi)
    )
    newly_na <- !is.na(kept_raw) & is.na(x$clean[[col]])

    expect_equal(sum(newly_na), sum(explained),
                 label = paste("values newly set to NA in", col))
  }
})

test_that("cleaning is reproducible: a fresh run writes identical files", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  derived <- here::here("data", "derived",
                        c("voles_clean.csv", "cleaning_log.csv", "exclusion_log.csv"))
  before <- unname(tools::md5sum(derived))
  callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"), wd = here::here(),
                 show = FALSE)
  expect_identical(unname(tools::md5sum(derived)), before)
})

test_that("clean data pass every rule in the agreed codebook", {
  skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data")
  clean_df <- readr::read_csv(
    clean_path,
    col_types = readr::cols(
      subject_id = readr::col_character(),
      sex = readr::col_character(),
      treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
      mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
      mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
      metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
      .default = readr::col_character()
    )
  )
  expect_equal(nrow(readr::problems(clean_df)), 0)

  # identifiers and labels
  expect_true(all(grepl("^V[0-9]{3}$", clean_df$subject_id)))
  expect_false(anyDuplicated(clean_df$subject_id) > 0)
  expect_true(all(clean_df$sex %in% c("M", "F")))
  expect_true(all(clean_df$treatment_arm %in% c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

  # ranges; a missing value is allowed, an out-of-range one is not
  in_range <- function(x, lo, hi) all(is.na(x) | (x >= lo & x <= hi))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$mass_pre_g, 15, 60))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$mass_post_g, 15, 60))
  expect_true(in_range(clean_df$metabolic_rate_post, 5, 30))
})

Instructor-led, about 5 minutes. Your instructor reveals the answer key and walks through each planted error. Open the list and, for each error, mark whether your logs record it.


The planted errors



Planted error
In your cleaning log?

treatment_arm label in upper case




sex spelled out

Check your understanding
Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?

Because AI tools cannot read CSV filesBecause missing-value codes, units and valid ranges are facts about how the data were collected; ranges read off the data include the very errors they are meant to detectBecause codebooks must be written in a specific file formatBecause the AI would take too long to profile the data

The agent reports “all tests pass”. What should you do next?

Nothing; the agent ran the testsRun the tests yourself in a fresh R session and read the diff; the agent's report is a claimAsk the agent to run them againDelete the tests, since they have done their job

How does the checksum test differ from the deny rule?

They are equivalent; one is redundantThe deny rule blocks one route (the agent's editing tools) before a change happens; the checksum detects a change by any route, after it happensThe checksum prevents edits; the deny rule only reports themThe deny rule works on GitHub; the checksum works only locally

Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipValidation: another view of the same rules





The last test in tests/test_cleaning.R already checks every rule in the agreed codebook. The template also ships the same rules as a report: scripts/functions/validate_voles.R, written with the pointblank package and run by scripts/02_validate.R. The live block does not use them. What they add is a second view: which rules the raw data break, and how often.
validate_voles.R was transcribed from the codebook by a person, not by the agent that writes the cleaning script. Each line is one rule, and interrogate() reports how many rows break it. (pointblank calls the object that holds the rules an “agent”; it has nothing to do with AI agents.)

# scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ----
# Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent
# that writes the cleaning script.

voles_col_types <- function() {
  readr::cols(
    subject_id = readr::col_character(),
    sex = readr::col_character(),
    treatment_arm = readr::col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(),
    mass_post_g = readr::col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(),
    .default = readr::col_character()
  )
}

validate_voles <- function(data, label) {
  data |>
    pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |>
    pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_in_set(
      columns = treatment_arm,
      set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g),
      left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::col_vals_between(
      columns = metabolic_rate_post,
      left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE
    ) |>
    pointblank::interrogate()
}

scripts/02_validate.R runs the rules on the raw data, which should fail (for example Raw data (expected to FAIL): 7 of 10 rules fail), and, once the cleaning has run, on the clean data, which should pass. It also lists any value that could not be read as a number: such a value would become NA and slip past the range rules. In an interactive session it opens the full report in the Viewer.
In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "02_validate.R"))


# scripts/02_validate.R ----
# Runs the codebook rules on the raw data (expected to FAIL) and, once
# 01_clean.R has run, on the clean data (expected to PASS). In an interactive
# session the full pointblank report also opens in the Viewer.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R"))

report_validation <- function(validation) {
  steps <- validation$validation_set
  n_failed <- sum(!steps$all_passed)
  cat(
    validation$label, ": ",
    if (n_failed == 0) "all rules pass" else paste(n_failed, "of", nrow(steps), "rules fail"),
    "\n",
    sep = ""
  )
  if (interactive()) print(validation)
  invisible(validation)
}

raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types())
# values that could not be read as numbers become NA and would pass the
# range rules, so list them
print(problems(raw_df), width = Inf)
report_validation(validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data (expected to FAIL)"))

clean_path <- here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv")
if (file.exists(clean_path)) {
  clean_df <- read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types())
  report_validation(validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data (expected to PASS)"))
}







Warning



na_pass = TRUE lets genuine missing values through, as the test’s range checks do. It would also let through a cleaning script that replaced every mass with NA. Rule checks alone cannot catch over-cleaning; the over-cleaning test in tests/test_cleaning.R can.











TipWrite the validation rules independently





Instead of using the shipped validate_voles.R, you can have the rules written by an AI that has never seen the cleaning code, for example a browser chat window given only the codebook:
Prompt (browser chat):
Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function
validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one
validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write
voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns,
with character as the default for anything else.

[paste docs/codebook.csv]
Compare what it writes with the shipped version. A rule it missed, or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook, is the kind of error the separate conversation is meant to expose.









TipRead the log yourself





The tests prove the log is truthful and complete; they cannot tell you whether a change was the right decision. The shipped scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R counts the changes by column and rule, and samples ten logged changes for you to check by eye against the raw file (View(), or Positron’s Data Explorer).

source(here::here("scripts", "03_audit_cleaning.R"))


# scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ----
# Purpose: read the cleaning log yourself. tests/test_cleaning.R already checks
# that the log is truthful and complete; it cannot tell you whether each change
# was the right decision. That is your job.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

cleaning_log_df <- read_csv(
  here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)

# 1. What kinds of change were made ----
cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE)

# 2. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ----
set.seed(2026)
cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10) |> print(width = Inf)










TipThe fresh-run checks, one by one





The test suite already reruns the cleaning in a fresh R session. To do the same checks by hand, commit the outputs, then in the R console:

renv::status()
callr::rscript(here::here("scripts", "01_clean.R"))

renv::status() should report a consistent state; if the agent used a package that is not in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., decide whether you want it and record it yourself with renv::snapshot(), as on Day 1 (the agent is denied renv.lock). After the callr::rscript() run the Git pane should show no changes.






NoteAt the command line





Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", Rscript -e "renv::status()", Rscript scripts/01_clean.R and git status --short data/derived, run after /exit or in a second Terminal tab. See checking work.












TipHow the template’s safeguards were made





The checksum. The template’s tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt was written once, from the shipped raw file, like this:

fs::dir_create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"))
writeLines(
  unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))),
  here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")
)

Do the same for your own raw data, then commit it. The template’s .gitattributes contains two lines, data/raw/** -text and data/derived/** -text, so git never changes the line endings of the data files when it checks them out. The tests compare those files byte for byte: the raw file against its checksum, and the clean files against a fresh run of the cleaning. Line endings converted by git, as can happen on Windows, would fail both tests with no real change to the data.
The deny rules. This is the .claude/settings.json in your workshop repository, the same file you read in Block 5:


{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "deny": [
      "Edit(/data/raw/**)",
      "Read(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)",
      "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)",
      "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)",
      "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)",
      "Edit(/renv.lock)",
      "Edit(/.github/**)",
      "Edit(/.claude/**)",
      "Edit(/.posit/**)",
      "Edit(/hooks/**)",
      "Read(/.Renviron)",
      "Read(/.env)"
    ]
  }
}


A leading / anchors each pattern to the project root. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write scripts/01_clean.R and data/derived/. To protect files of your own, add rules with /permissions. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the Going further section of Block 5 instead.






Warning



What each control covers. The deny rule blocks the agent’s file-editing tools, and shell output redirects such as > file. It does not cover R code the agent runs: an R script that writes to data/raw/ is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by any route, but only after the fact. Use both: one prevents, the other detects. A deny rule on reading does not stop data reaching the model provider by other routes; see Block 3.


The skill. The skill ships in .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/. To use it in another project, download it and unzip it into that project’s .agents/skills/ (unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills"))), then copy the folder into .claude/skills/ with fs::dir_copy().

Glossary




term
definition



checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.


codebook
A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.


lockfile
The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.


sentinel value
A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.

Step 1: snapshot, refactor and test with the skill
scripts/05_analysis.R summarises post-treatment metabolic rate (mean, SD and count) by treatment arm and sex. Notice one thing and leave it alone: one animal has no metabolic_rate_post and there is no na.rm, so the mean and the SD for its group are both NA.
The shipped skillA folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description. characterisation-refactor does the work in order and stops for you after each part.






TipReference: the code you will refactor, and the loading it relies on






# scripts/05_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R"))

metabolic_summary <- voles |>
  group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
    sd_rate   = sd(metabolic_rate_post),
    n         = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )


# scripts/04_load_data.R ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles <- load_voles()


# scripts/functions/load_voles.R ----
load_voles <- function() {
  readr::read_csv(
    here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
    col_types = readr::cols(
      subject_id          = readr::col_character(),
      sex                 = readr::col_character(),
      treatment_arm       = readr::col_character(),
      mass_pre_g          = readr::col_double(),
      mass_post_g         = readr::col_double(),
      metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double()
    )
  )
}






One request, one commit, one diff, one test run (20 minutes)


Goal: one request to the skill, ending with a committed reference, a refactored function and a protected test that proves the output unchanged, so that you can restructure working code without fearing that its results moved.
Start state: Step 0 done, Git pane clean; /clear any earlier conversation in Claude Code.
1. Ask.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/characterisation-refactor Move the summary in scripts/05_analysis.R into
summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R.
The skill shows its plan as a message and waits. Read it, then reply in Claude Code: Yes, go ahead, or say what to change. The plan should capture the reference first.
2. Approve the capture, then commit the reference. The skill asks to run tests/make_reference.R. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can: it saves the original code’s output before anything changes. When the skill stops, the Git pane should show only tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds as new: commit it (“Capture reference output before refactoring”) and tell the agent to carry on.
3. Read the diff when it stops again. Diff each changed file in the Git pane, looking for anything beyond moving the code into the function, then tell it to carry on and write the test.
4. Protect the new test. The skill runs only its new test file, reports the output and stops. Now protect that test, so the agent cannot later change it to make a failing run pass: in /permissions, add the deny rule Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R), saved to the project’s shared settings file, .claude/settings.json.
5. Run the whole suite. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so that nothing left in your session can make a test pass, then in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))







Test
Passing proves




test_summary_functions.R (the agent’s)
the function reproduces your reference exactly



test_reference_guard.R (shipped)
the agent’s test reads your reference file and calls the function, and the reference is unchanged since your commit



test_controls.R (shipped)
every deny rule is in place, including your new one



The guard cannot tell whether numbers were also typed into the test; reading the test can. Other blocks’ tests pass or skip.
You are done when the suite has no failures and the Git pane shows only the function, 05_analysis.R, the new test and .claude/settings.json as changed. Commit them.
If it goes wrong: see Fixes for Step 1 below the task, or switch to checkpoint-refactor.
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?








NoteFixes for Step 1







The capture. If the agent declines to run make_reference.R, or a guard hook from Block 5 blocks it, capture it yourself: restart R, run source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R")), commit the .rds, and tell the agent the reference is committed.

Changed files. If anything other than the .rds changed before your commit, Revert it and ask again.

Row order. A failure on row order, not values, means the function used .by without sorting: ask the agent to add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex).

The new rule. If test_controls.R says the test is unprotected, check the rule’s spelling in /permissions. If settings.json is not in the Git pane, the rule went to the local file: remove it there and add it again, choosing .claude/settings.json. If the agent offers to add the rule itself, refuse: it is yours to add.

Otherwise, Revert the agent’s files and ask again, or switch to checkpoint-refactor.









NoteHow it works: the capture, the settings file and the test rules





The capture. The skill runs make_reference.R only if no reference exists yet and scripts/ has no uncommitted changes, and never again after that. Who runs the capture script matters less than when: before any code changes, from a script you trust, and committed by you. After that, git and test_reference_guard.R notice any change to the reference.
The shared settings file. /permissions can save a rule to .claude/settings.json, which you commit, or to the local .claude/settings.local.json, which git ignores, so a rule saved there would never reach a commit. The rule takes effect at once.
No known-answer case yet. Your AGENTS.md asks for a known-answer test with every new function. The skill’s test rules take precedence: a characterisation test compares with the original output, and known-answer tests come in Step 2, once you decide the behaviour should change. The skill also leaves the whole suite and the settings to you.









NoteWhat the skill tells the agent (characterisation-refactor/SKILL.md)







---
name: characterisation-refactor
description: >-
  Refactors working R analysis code into documented functions under a
  characterisation test, so the output is proved unchanged. Use when asked to
  functionalise, refactor or tidy a script whose output must not change.
  Not for fixing bugs or changing results.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Refactor under a characterisation test

## The reference comes from the original code, and the user commits it
The frozen reference in tests/fixtures/ is written by the user's own capture
script (tests/make_reference.R) from the original, unchanged code, and the
user commits it before anything else changes. A reference made after the code
has changed proves nothing.
- Run tests/make_reference.R at most once, in step 2 below, and only if no
  reference exists yet and git status shows no uncommitted changes under
  scripts/. Never run it at any other time, and never edit the capture script.
- Never edit, regenerate or delete anything under tests/fixtures/.
- If a reference already exists, use it as it is.

## Procedure
1. Present a plan: whether a reference must be captured, the code to move,
   the function name and file, and the test file. Wait for the user to
   confirm.
2. Capture only, if no reference exists. Run git status; if anything under
   scripts/ has uncommitted changes, stop and ask. Otherwise run
   Rscript tests/make_reference.R, report the file it wrote, and stop: ask
   the user to commit it before you change any code. Do not commit it
   yourself.
3. Refactor only. Write the function in scripts/functions/ with a roxygen2
   block and an argument check, and make the original script call it. Do not
   write or edit tests in this step. Stop and let the user review the diff.
4. Test only. Write tests/test_<functions file>.R (for
   scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, that is
   tests/test_summary_functions.R). Start it with library(testthat) and
   testthat::local_edition(3), source the function files with
   here::here(), read the reference from tests/fixtures/ with readRDS(), and
   compare it with the function's output using expect_equal(). Never
   hard-code expected values, and never reimplement the computation inside
   the test. Include an expect_error() test showing that the argument check
   rejects data with a required column missing. This step's rules take
   precedence over any project instruction to add known-answer tests: those
   come later, if the user decides the behaviour should change.
5. Run only the new test file in a fresh R session, for example
   Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_summary_functions.R')", and
   report the output verbatim. Then stop: the user protects the new test and
   runs the whole suite. Do not change any settings file.

## Rules
- If the test fails, report the difference. Never change the test, the
  tolerance or the reference to make it pass.
- Sort the output rows explicitly with dplyr::arrange() on the grouping
  columns, so the order never depends on how the data happen to be stored.
- Do not change behaviour, including how missing values are handled. A
  passing test shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct; list
  anything that looks wrong for the user to decide.











TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant. It reads the same skill from .agents/skills/. Use it in Normal mode and run the same test suite; with no path rules for edits, the Git pane and test_reference_guard.R are what protect the reference.

text:
Step 2: unchanged is not correct
Your test passes, including the NA mean and SD for one group. If you wanted the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along, and a characterisation test cannot tell: it compares against the past, not against the truth. Judging the behaviour correct is a separate step, and it is yours.


Decide, change, and test the change independently (12 minutes)


Goal: change the behaviour on purpose, prove it with a known-answer test, and record why the reference changed, so that anyone reading the history sees a decision, not drift.
1. Decide. The mean and standard deviation should use measured animals only, and the count should not include the unmeasured animal (n() counts rows).
2. Ask for the change and a known-answer test.
Prompt (Claude Code):
In summarise_metabolic_rate(), compute the mean and SD with na.rm = TRUE, and
report n_used and n_missing instead of n. Add a known-answer test on a small
tibble in a new file, tests/test_known_answers.R, and show me how you worked
out the expected values. Do not change tests/test_summary_functions.R.
A known-answer testA test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged. checks the new behaviour against a result you can work out by hand. Check the arithmetic yourself: the mean of 10, 14 and a missing value is 12, from two measured animals.


A function and test you should converge on


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_used    = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


# tests/test_known_answers.R ----
library(testthat)
testthat::local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", {
  toy_df <- tibble::tibble(
    treatment_arm       = c("Control", "Control", "Control"),
    sex                 = c("F", "F", "F"),
    metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA)
  )
  result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df)

  expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12)
  expect_equal(result$n_used, 2)
  expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1)
})


3. Watch the characterisation test fail, correctly. Run the suite as in Step 1: the output has changed, so it fails; the known-answer test passes. If the agent asks to run make_reference.R, refuse: re-capturing is your decision.
4. Re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision. Restart R, then in the R console:

source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R"))

5. Commit, then run the suite. Commit the reference, the function and the new test file with a message that says why, for example “Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing”. Only then run the suite as in Step 1: test_reference_guard.R fails while the new reference is uncommitted.
Re-capturing is safe here for three reasons: you decided it, a known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why.
6. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed) and commit it.
You are done when the whole suite passes again, the re-captured reference is committed with its reason, and your AI-log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if the known-answer test fails, the arithmetic or the function is wrong; read both before changing either. Short of time? Switch to checkpoint-refactor, which has Step 2 done.








NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: let an agent snapshot, refactor and test working analysis code with one request, trusted because the reference came from the original code, committed by you before anything changed, and a shipped guard test checks that the agent’s test reads it.

Check: the whole test suite; the diff in the Git pane; the arithmetic of the known-answer test.

Reproduce: the suite passes after Session → Restart R, with nothing changed under tests/fixtures/.

Record: the re-captured reference is a decision with a commit message that says why; your AI-log line records the request, whether the test passed first time, and what you changed.

A characterisation test passes after a refactor. What has it established?

That the function's output is correctThat the function's output is the same as the original code's output, whether or not that output was correctThat the function is faster than the original codeThat the original code had no bugs

Why must the reference be captured and committed before the refactor starts?

Because agents cannot write .rds filesBecause git cannot track .rds files once the code has changedBecause a reference captured after the code changed is produced by the code under test, so it can only confirm that the code agrees with itselfBecause the reference would be too large

The shipped deny rules protect tests/fixtures/ in Claude Code. Once you have committed the reference, which action could still change it?

Asking the agent to edit the .rds file with its editing toolThe agent running tests/make_reference.R again through the shell (git and test_reference_guard.R would show it)Opening the .rds file in the IDERunning the test suite with testthat::test_dir()
