title: Block 8: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged
text:
Going further (not covered live)
This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you.






TipWhat the skill does, step by step





The skill turns a capture and two prompts into one request. Written out by hand, the capture is yours: restart R, run source(here::here("tests", "make_reference.R")), and commit the .rds. The two prompts are below. Splitting the work matters: a single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once, producing a passing test that proves nothing.
Prompt 1: the refactor only.
Move the computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented function
summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a
roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call the new function
instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch
anything under tests/.
Prompt 2: the test only.
Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with
summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal().

Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not
run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you
generate proves nothing.
Before trusting a passing test you would check four things: the test reads the .rds rather than hard-coding numbers; it calls the function rather than reimplementing the pipeline; nothing changed under tests/fixtures/; and the agent’s commands (shown in the conversation) include no run of tests/make_reference.R after the capture you committed. The shipped test_reference_guard.R checks part of this automatically: that the test reads the .rds and calls the function, and that nothing under tests/fixtures/ has changed since your commit. It cannot tell whether numbers were also typed into the test or the pipeline copied into it, so read the test once yourself; the fourth check is why you read approval requests in Manual mode.






Warning



What a deny rule does not cover. Claude Code’s deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, and to shell output redirects such as > file, but not to R code or most other commands it runs. The skill relies on that to take the first snapshot; an agent that ran Rscript tests/make_reference.R again later would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git, and test_reference_guard.R, are the final checks.


To use the skill in your own projects, download it and unzip it into your project’s .agents/skills/ (and copy it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code):


 Download characterisation-refactor.zip











TipWithout an agent: write the function and the test yourself





Everything here is written by you; only make_reference.R and the data are shipped. First capture and commit the reference as above. A tidy refactor naturally reaches for the modern .by argument. Write this first attempt in a new file, scripts/functions/summary_functions.R:


First attempt (deliberately incomplete)


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ----
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    )
}


Now write the test and run it:

# tests/test_summary_functions.R ----
library(testthat)
local_edition(3)
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", {
  reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds"))
  expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8)
})

Run it as in Step 1: restart R, then testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")).


What happened

It fails, and not on the numbers. .by returns the groups in order of first appearance; the reference, made with group_by(), has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, and expect_equal() reports a mismatch. Add dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) to the end of the pipeline and the test passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it.
If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex).

Do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals: a test that compares the function with numbers you transcribed proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must read the .rds.


Refactored function, and the script that calls it


# scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ----
#' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and
#'   metabolic_rate_post.
#' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both,
#'   giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows.
summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))
  required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post")
  missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "`data` is missing required column(s): ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  data |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post),
      sd_rate   = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post),
      n         = dplyr::n(),
      .by       = c(treatment_arm, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)
}


# scripts/05_analysis.R: after refactoring ----
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "04_load_data.R"))
source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R"))

metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles)











TipProtecting the new test by editing the settings file





/permissions writes this same file when you choose the shared settings file. The same rule can be added by hand: open .claude/settings.json in the editor and add "Edit(/tests/test_summary_functions.R)" to the deny list, minding the comma after the line before. Claude Code reloads the file without a restart. Either way, commit the file, so the rule travels with the repository. test_controls.R checks the rule is there.









TipThe review gate





Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely. On GitHub, a pull request that changes a file under tests/ can be held until the code owner reviews it. How to set up CODEOWNERS and branch protection is in the Going further section of Block 5.









TipReuse the skill on a second step





A skill earns its keep the second time you use it.


Reuse the skill (15 minutes)


Goal: use the skill on a second step, with a reference you captured and committed yourself, so that you know its discipline holds on code it was not written for.
1. Capture a reference yourself first. Pick a second step: the plotting code in scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R, which you made in Block 3 (it is on checkpoint-skills if you need it), or a step from your own project. The skill runs only the shipped make_reference.R, so for any other step the capture is yours: write a small capture script modelled on it, run it after restarting R, commit its output in tests/fixtures/, and protect the script with /permissions (choosing .claude/settings.json, as in Step 1).
2. Invoke the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/characterisation-refactor Functionalise the step in
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that I captured in tests/fixtures/.
Start with the plan.
3. Compare. Did the agent still stop between the refactor and the test? Run the whole suite, and check the Git pane for anything changed under tests/fixtures/.
You are done when the whole suite has no failures and the Git pane shows nothing changed under tests/fixtures/ since you committed the new reference.











TipAn asynchronous agent: the Copilot cloud agent





The same work can be handed to an agent that runs remotely while you do something else. It works on a branch in GitHub’s infrastructure and returns a pull request. Before you start, check that your Copilot plan includes the cloud agent, that copilot-setup-steps.yml is on your default branch (see The environment the test runs in below), and that the repository has the review gate from The review gate on GitHub in the Going further section of Block 5 (its CODEOWNERS already covers tests/ and .github/).
Keep the two-step discipline by writing two issues, and assign the second only after you have reviewed and merged the first.
Issue 1
Title: Move the metabolic-rate summary into a function

Move the summary computation in scripts/05_analysis.R into a documented
function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R,
with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 05_analysis.R call it.

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/.
- The output must be identical to the current output, including row order
  and the existing NA values.
Issue 2 (after Issue 1 is merged)
Title: Add a characterisation test for summarise_metabolic_rate()

Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source
scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, and
compare summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) with
tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds using expect_equal().

Acceptance criteria:
- Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do
  not run tests/make_reference.R.
- Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description.
Assign each issue to Copilot. When a pull request arrives:

Open Files changed. Confirm that only the expected files changed. A change under tests/fixtures/ or .github/ should not merge, and CODEOWNERS will in any case require your review for it.
Read the test against the four checks in What the skill does, step by step above; test_reference_guard.R automates part of them.
Check that the r-checks run on the pull request passed.
Pull the branch and run the test on your own machine. The agent’s report that “tests pass” is its claim; your run is the check.

If something is wrong, comment on the pull request to ask for a revision, or close it. Nothing reaches main until you merge.









TipThe environment the test runs in





A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in load_voles() handle the finest-grained part. The R version and the package set are handled by two GitHub Actions workflows. Neither ships with the template: to use them, create each file in .github/workflows/.
r-checks.yml is the independent check. It runs the tests from a clean checkout on every push to main and on every pull request:
name: r-checks
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)'
It is independent of your machine and of the agent’s environment, but it is not tamper-proof. A pull request can change the workflow file or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection (set up in Block 5’s Going further) are what make a passing run meaningful: you review every change to those paths before it merges.
copilot-setup-steps.yml builds the environment the Copilot cloud agent works in. Following GitHub’s documented pattern:
name: "Copilot Setup Steps"

# Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds,
# and can be run by hand from the Actions tab.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

jobs:
  # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it.
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: "4.5.2"   # match the R version in renv.lock
          use-public-rspm: true
      - name: Restore packages from renv.lock
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
Four requirements, each with a different failure mode:


The job name must be exactly copilot-setup-steps. If it is not, Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function.

The file must be on the default branch, or it is not used.

The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux or Windows 64-bit. The cloud agent does not support macOS runners; Ubuntu is the usual choice for R.

The lockfile must be restored. If it restores the wrong versions, the failure is quiet: tests run and pass against different package behaviour. The frozen reference then certifies sameness against the wrong baseline.

When the agent’s test run and the independent r-checks run disagree, suspect the environment before you suspect the code.

text:
Glossary




term
definition



characterisation test
A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.


deny rule
A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.


known-answer test
A test that checks code against a result worked out independently, for example by hand. It can show code is correct, where a characterisation test only shows it is unchanged.


skill
A folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
Activity: The context demonstration
Inline completion is the simplest kind of assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files.: grey “ghost text” appears as you type, and you accept it with Tab, reject it with Esc, or carry on typing. By the end of this page you will know how to get useful suggestions every time: write a specific comment just before the cursor. Claude Code has no inline completion, so this page uses GitHub Copilot instead.
Self-study: about 25 minutes, after the workshop day. Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, signed in to GitHub Copilot (if you are not, do the GitHub Copilot step in Setting up Claude Code first).

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
The context demonstration (10 minutes)


Goal: see how the code above the cursor changes Copilot’s suggestion for the same comment, so that you know what to put in a script to get useful suggestions.
Start state: your workshop repository open, signed in to GitHub Copilot.
The data are voles_metabolism.csv: a synthetic trial in 72 voles, with columns subject_id, sex, treatment_arm, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g and metabolic_rate_post. The names were chosen so that no model has seen them before.
0. Check that Copilot works. This command creates the scratch/ folder and this page’s practice script, and opens it:
In the R console:

usethis::edit_file("scratch/completions.R")

In scratch/completions.R, type # Calculate the mean of 1 to 100. Within a few seconds you should see ghost text such as mean(1:100); if not, press Enter and wait.
1. No context. Delete everything in scratch/completions.R. Type only this comment, and wait.
In scratch/completions.R:

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment

Note the suggestion. With no data and no column names in view, the model has to guess.
2. Context in the file. Empty scratch/completions.R again. Type the lines below down to glimpse(voles), and run them, so that voles is loaded. Then type the same comment on a new line, and wait.
In scratch/completions.R:

# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
# 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes
# Native pipe |>, tidyverse

library(tidyverse)

voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"))
glimpse(voles)

# calculate the mean change in mass by treatment



A typical good result


voles |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |>
  summarise(
    mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = treatment_arm
  )

The exact form varies between people and sessions.

Compare the two suggestions. Did the second use real column names? Did it compute post minus pre?
You are done when you can say what the second suggestion had that the first did not.
If it goes wrong: if no ghost text appears, check that you are signed in to GitHub and the set-up route for your IDE (in Set-up routes, plans and data, just after this task), then type the comment again on a new line; if scratch/completions.R stops running, Session → Restart R and run it from the top.








NoteSet-up routes, plans and data







RStudio: enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio’s options and sign in to GitHub.

Positron: choose GitHub Copilot as the completions provider (see Positron’s completions documentation).

Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid plans do not meter them. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in Block 3 apply here too.









TipUsing another tool





Use one completion provider at a time, so you know which tool made each suggestion.
Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions (RStudio and Positron): in RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button (it needs a Posit AI account); in Positron, choose it as the completions provider. Posit AI does not meter completions. Unlike Copilot, it also sees your live R session: the columns of loaded data frames, the functions you have defined and the packages you have loaded. So, in the context demonstration:

restart R (Session → Restart R) before step 1, so that “no context” means none;
after step 2, keep voles loaded, empty scratch/completions.R and type only the comment from step 1. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, they came from your session, not from the file.

VS Code: select Use AI Features from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub. As in Positron, Copilot may also use other open tabs.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
The context principle
A suggestion can only use what is in the model’s context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window. when it is made. Copilot fills that window mainly from the current file, and above all from the comment just before the cursor. In Positron it may also use other open tabs. It does not see your R session.

title: Self-study: Inline completions
text:
Activity: Build a small analysis


Build a small analysis (10 minutes)


Goal: extend scratch/completions.R into a short analysis that reruns, deciding on every suggestion yourself, so that no suggestion enters your code unchecked.
Start state: scratch/completions.R with the step 2 code from the demonstration, and voles loaded.
For each step, write the comment first, then accept, modify or reject the suggestion, and note which you did in a comment under the code, for example # modified: added n(). The note is what makes you notice an unchecked acceptance.
0. Derived column. Add mass_change_g (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g) to voles as a column. Steps 1 and 2 need it there, not only inside a summary.
1. Summary table. The mean and standard deviation of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with the number of observations per cell.
2. Plot. mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm.
You are done when steps 0 to 2 each have a note (accepted, modified or rejected), and scratch/completions.R, saved and run from the top in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. (Session → Restart R), produces the table and the plot without error.
If it goes wrong: delete the last suggestion you accepted, and write a more specific comment naming the data frame and its columns.


An example


# Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

voles <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    subject_id = col_character(),
    sex = col_character(),
    treatment_arm = col_character(),
    mass_pre_g = col_double(),
    mass_post_g = col_double(),
    metabolic_rate_post = col_double()
  )
) |>
  mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g)

# mean and SD of mass_change_g by treatment_arm and sex, with n per cell
voles |>
  summarise(
    mean_change_g = mean(mass_change_g),
    sd_change_g = sd(mass_change_g),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)
  ) |>
  arrange(treatment_arm, sex)

# mass_change_g against metabolic_rate_post, coloured by treatment_arm
ggplot(voles, aes(metabolic_rate_post, mass_change_g, colour = treatment_arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Metabolic rate (post-treatment)", y = "Change in mass (g)")

The plot drops the one animal with no metabolic rate and says so in a warning: read it rather than ignore it.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: steer inline completion with a specific comment and the right code above the cursor, trusted because you decided on every suggestion and your script runs from a fresh R session.

Check: accept, modify or reject every suggestion deliberately.

Reproduce: good suggestions come from context in the file, so keep that context in your script, where it reruns.

Record: nothing to log for practice code in scratch/. When completions write code you keep, add a line to your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README., in the form from Block 3.

Glossary




term
definition



AI-use log
A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.


assistant
Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.


context window
The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.


fresh R session
An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
text:
Telling the AI how to behave
You will hand a script to an AI reviewer and grade what it finds. Because you already know this script’s twelve problems, you can measure the machine rather than trust it. First, note your answer to a question the self-check returns to: if an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?
Self-study: about 40 minutes, after the workshop day. Start state: your workshop repository open, Git pane clean. It does not matter which blocks you finished, and there is no checkpoint branch.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
section: Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review
text:
Part 1: What AI is, and is not, good for in code review
⏱ ~5 minutes
An AI reviewer reads every line and never tires, but it sounds equally sure whether it is right or wrong. Here is where to expect help, on the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023):



AI capability mapped onto the four Rs

R
AI is likely to be...
Why



Reported
Useful for drafting
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.


Run
Strong, if it can execute
An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.


Reliable
Weak
Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.





The rule: treat every AI finding as a claim to check, and the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.
Run your saved review prompt on a script before you share it, and spend your own attention on the Reliable questions.






TipBackground: what the evidence says





Used that way, AI review is reliably good for:

summarising what an unfamiliar script does;
flagging missing documentation, unexplained filters and hard-coded paths;
finding run errors, when it can actually execute the code;
a second pair of eyes that never tires on line 300.

In software engineering, developers acted on about three-quarters of an AI reviewer’s comments but saw only minor gains in quality, and the reviewer did worse when it was not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan et al., 2025; Cihan, 2025). Nobody has measured it on analysis scripts like this one, which is what you will do.









Note



Before you start (answer for yourself)
“If an AI code reviewer told you your analysis was clean, would you trust it enough to submit?”
A: Yes, it read every line B: Only if I had also read it myself C: No, I would trust my own review over the AI’s D: I would trust it for Run, not for Reliable
Note your answer; the self-check at the end returns to it.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
text:
Write the review prompt (7 minutes)


Goal: a review prompt with all four parts, saved in your workshop repository, so that you can reuse it on your own scripts after the course.
1. Start from the draft below and check it has all four parts. “Review my code” alone gets a vague, generous review; a good review prompt has:






Part
Why




A role and a standard: “a critical reviewer applying the four Rs”
Gives the output a structure you can check



The intended analysis: the model from the OSF page, with TO a count and block B a random effect
Without it, the AI cannot see that a Gaussian lmer() is the wrong family (P10)



No flattery: line number, which R, severity, a fix
Keeps it to findings you can act on



Honest uncertainty: “NEEDS HUMAN CHECK” instead of guessing
Shows you where to look yourself



2. Choose your version. The line about the 9999 sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis. tells the reviewer something the script alone cannot. Keep it, or delete it to see what the reviewer finds unaided; doing both, as two runs, shows the difference the line makes. Everything else stays the same.
3. Keep it. In your workshop repository, run usethis::edit_file("docs/review-prompt.md") in the R console, paste your prompt, save, and commit it from the Git pane. You will reuse it after the course.
You are done when your prompt has all four elements and is committed as docs/review-prompt.md.


Working draft

Prompt (Claude Code):
You are a critical code reviewer for an evolutionary-biology journal.
Review ANALYSIS.R using the four Rs: Reported, Run, Reliable, Reproducible.

The intended analysis (from the pre-registration) is:
  total offspring (TO, a count: non-negative integer, often overdispersed)
  modelled as TO ~ strain * diet + (1 | B), with block B as a random effect.

Rules:
- Do NOT praise the code. Report only problems.
- For each issue: line number(s), which R it violates, severity
  (critical / high / medium), and a concrete one-line fix.
- The raw data use 9999 as a "not recorded" code. Check whether this is
  handled.                                <- delete for a run without it
- Flag anything you CANNOT determine by reading alone as "NEEDS HUMAN
  CHECK" rather than guessing.
- If you are uncertain about a finding, say so explicitly.
Organise your output by the four Rs.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
text:
Running the review
For a comparison with and without the 9999 line to work, the agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. must see the script and nothing else; with the data it would find the 9999 code by itself. That is why ~/ai-review holds only ANALYSIS.R. The chat route is in Using another tool, after the task.


Run the review (10 minutes)


Goal: an AI review of ANALYSIS.R, made from the script alone and saved as ~/ai-review/review_claude.md, so that you can grade it against problems you already know.
Start state: your review prompt committed as docs/review-prompt.md in your workshop repository.
1. Get the script into a new folder. In the R console of any project:

review_dir <- usethis::create_project("~/ai-review", open = FALSE)
download.file("https://osf.io/download/3x6hb/",
              file.path(review_dir, "ANALYSIS.R"), mode = "wb")

create_project() prints where it made the folder. Open that folder in a new window: in RStudio, File → Open Project in New Session; in Positron, File → New Window, then open the folder there.
2. Start Claude Code there, in Manual mode. In the new window’s Terminal tab:
claude
This folder has none of your workshop settings, so check that the mode shown is Manual (default); if it is not, press Shift+Tab until it is.
3. Ask for the review. Type /plan, a space, then paste your prompt. Starting with /plan keeps it to reading. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. If it asks whether to proceed, choose No, keep planning.
4. Save the review. plan mode writes no files, so save it yourself: run usethis::edit_file("~/ai-review/review_claude.md") in the R console, paste the whole review and save.
You are done when ~/ai-review/review_claude.md holds the agent’s whole review.
If it goes wrong: if the download fails, download ANALYSIS.R from the OSF project in your browser into the folder create_project() reported. If Claude Code mentions AGENTS.md or the voles data, you started it in your workshop window: /exit, switch windows and start again. If you have no agent, use the chat route in Using another tool.








NoteHow it works







The new folder. create_project() gives the folder an .Rproj or .here file, so that here::here() works there.

The mode. With none of your workshop settings, Claude Code may start in auto. In Manual (default) it asks before doing anything.

/plan. Plan mode keeps the agent to reading (rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. 2 in Block 3), and writes no files.










TipUsing another tool





Doing the Claude Code route and the chat route both shows the difference between a chat window, which can only predict whether the script runs, and an agent, which can run it (see the stretch).
Posit Assistant. Open ~/ai-review in RStudio or Positron and switch Posit Assistant to Ask mode, so it can read but not change anything, then give it your review prompt. For the stretch below, use Normal mode, so it asks before running anything.
Chat window. Paste the whole of ANALYSIS.R into any chat window, followed by your review prompt. Paste the script only, not the data. A chat window cannot run anything, but its answer to “does this run?” can read as though it did: ask “what would prevent this running?” instead.
Either way, save the review as in step 4, naming the file after the tool (for example ~/ai-review/review_chat.md).









TipStretch: let it run the script





An agent that can run R turns the Run question from a prediction into evidence. In the same Claude Code session, after you have saved your review, check that the mode shown is Manual (default): after /plan it may still be in plan, so press Shift+Tab until it shows Manual and it asks before running anything. The folder has no data, and for this it needs none: the run stops before the script reads any. Where it stops, and why, is the finding.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Run ANALYSIS.R from a fresh R session with Rscript and report the exact
output and any errors. Do not install packages; if a package is missing,
report which one. Do not edit any file.
Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Then read the output. “The script runs” counts only if you can see the command and its output in the conversation; without them it is a claimed executionA statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.. A missing package is a finding about your machine, not about the code.

Check your understanding
An AI reviewer reports that ANALYSIS.R “runs without errors”. What do you need before treating that as evidence?

Nothing; the model has read every lineA second AI reviewer's agreementThe command it ran and the output it saw, from a fresh R session; without them the statement is a predictionA statement of confidence from the model

text:
Going further
This material goes beyond the review itself. Work through it if it is useful to you.






TipCopilot code review on a pull request





If your repository is on GitHub, open a pull request containing ANALYSIS.R and request Copilot as a reviewer. Its comments appear on the changed lines, like a colleague’s. It reads the repository’s instruction files (.github/copilot-instructions.md, or AGENTS.md as in Block 4), but none of those exist in ~/ai-review yet. To have Copilot apply the standard from your review prompt, add your review rules (the four Rs, the intended analysis, no praise, NEEDS HUMAN CHECK) to .github/copilot-instructions.md in that repository before you request the review.









TipGenerating the README with AI





Self-study: about 20 minutes.
The second deliverable is the documentation that makes Reported and Run answerable: a README. You are provided with the research-readme skill: a SKILL.md, two helper scripts and a template.
Add the data first. A README describes the data as well as the code, so ~/ai-review now needs them. In the R console of the ai-review window:

download.file("https://osf.io/download/xke5g/",
              here::here("celegans_repro_raw.csv"), mode = "wb")
download.file("https://osf.io/download/6ev3g/",
              here::here("celegans_repro_final.csv"), mode = "wb")

Install the skill before you start. Download the bundle, then unzip it into ~/ai-review at .agents/skills/: in the R console of the ai-review window, run unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills")) and choose the downloaded file. The folder .agents/skills/research-readme/ should then contain SKILL.md, scripts/ and references/.


 Download research-readme.zip




Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot read .agents/skills/ directly.

Claude Code reads .claude/skills/. Link or copy the folder there, as described in Block 4.

Chat window: you do not need to install anything. You will run the two scripts yourself and paste the template into the chat.

Check that the skill is visible before going on. In Claude Code, type / and look for research-readme. In any tool, the test is behaviour: when you invoke /research-readme in Pass 2, its first reply should be the numbered plan that the skill’s “Before executing” section requires. If it is not, the skill did not load.
Put the folder under version control first. ~/ai-review is not a git repository, so there would be nothing to compare the README against. With ~/ai-review open in RStudio or Positron, run usethis::use_git() in the R console and let it make the first commit.
You run this in two passes. The first shows the failure; the second shows the fix.
Pass 1: README from the AI alone (self-study: about 4 minutes)
Give the AI only ANALYSIS.R and the data, and ask for a README with no constraints:
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository from ANALYSIS.R and
the two CSV files. Show it in your reply; do not write any file.
In a chat window, paste ANALYSIS.R and the data after the same request.
The result reads as complete. It will assign plausible units, describe variables it cannot have verified, and may state package versions it has no way to know. Note what it asserts about the variables and dependencies; Pass 2 replaces each guess with a fact you generate.
Pass 2: README from verifiable inputs
The skill’s rules are that the AI must not fabricate metadata, and that automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. So you generate the facts mechanically, and the AI only assembles and phrases them.
Step 1: Generate the inputs yourself (R, not AI)
In the R console of the ai-review window (so that here::here() points at ~/ai-review, not at your workshop repository):

skill_dir <- here::here(".agents", "skills", "research-readme", "scripts")

source(file.path(skill_dir, "describe_csv.R"))
# type, missing count and range per column, printed in full for pasting
describe_project_csvs(here::here()) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

source(file.path(skill_dir, "scan_packages.R"))
print_lockfile(here::here("renv.lock"))  # R and package versions, or a finding

This project has no renv.lock. scan_packages.R reports that as an explicit finding rather than an error, and the README must say so. You cannot pin versions you never recorded.
Look at the offspring column in the summary: its range will read something like 2 to 9999. The 9999 code (P8) is a real number in the file, and the summary reports it without judgement. Judging plausibility is your job. That honest, uninterpreted range is the visible trace of the sentinel.
Step 2: Hand the AI the specification and the inputs
Agent path: in Manual mode, as in Run the review, invoke /research-readme and let its five stages run. The skill shows its plan as a message and waits. Read it, then reply in Claude Code: Yes, go ahead, or say what to change. It will ask you for what it cannot find.
Chat path: paste the structure from references/readme_template.md and the output you just generated, with this prompt:
Prompt (chat window):
Draft a research README.md for this analysis repository, using exactly the
sections in the template I paste below, in order.

Use ONLY the facts I provide. Do not invent DOIs, ORCIDs, units or package
versions. Where a value is missing, insert a visible placeholder:
  **TODO: supply [field]: not provided**

Per-column summaries: [paste describe_project_csvs() output]
Dependencies: [paste print_lockfile() output]
Run order: ANALYSIS.R (the only analysis script in the folder).

Add an AI declaration stating that an AI assisted in drafting this README,
naming the model and today's date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere.


Audit the README (10 minutes)


Goal: check the Pass 2 README against three of the skill’s rules, so that you know which of its statements you could put your name to.
Audit the draft against three of the skill’s rules:


No fabrication. Pick three facts. Can you trace each to an input you gave? If not, it is invented.

Describe, do not interpret. Did the AI assign units or meanings you did not supply? Did the 2 to 9999 range survive, or was it “tidied” into something plausible and wrong?

README only. The Git pane should show that nothing except README.md changed since the commit you made before Pass 1.

Note the worst fabrication or interpretation you caught, and whether the README’s offspring range alone would have led you back to P8. The AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. should say no more than you told it.
You are done when each of the three rules is marked kept or broken, you have noted the worst fabrication or interpretation, and the Git pane shows only README.md changed.


The skill bundle
The bundle you downloaded above is reproduced here for reference; you do not need to edit it. Read it before you use it, as you would any skill you did not write.
research-readme/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── describe_csv.R
│   └── scan_packages.R
└── references/
    └── readme_template.md






Notescripts/describe_csv.R






# describe_csv.R ----
# Purpose: one row per column of a CSV file: name, the type readr assigns,
# missing-value count, and a brief range (numeric) or distinct-value count
# (other). Describes; does not interpret.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 2.

describe_range <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return("all values missing")
  }
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    return(paste(min(x, na.rm = TRUE), "to", max(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  }
  paste(dplyr::n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), "distinct values")
}

# one-row-per-column summary of a single CSV ----
describe_csv <- function(path) {
  stopifnot(is.character(path), length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  data_df <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  tibble::tibble(
    file        = basename(path),
    column      = names(data_df),
    type        = purrr::map_chr(data_df, \(x) class(x)[1]),
    n_missing   = purrr::map_int(data_df, \(x) sum(is.na(x))),
    range       = purrr::map_chr(data_df, describe_range),
    # completed by the user during Stage 2:
    description = NA_character_,
    unit        = NA_character_
  )
}

# describe every CSV in a project, skipping renv and git folders ----
describe_project_csvs <- function(project_dir) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(project_dir))
  csv_paths <- list.files(
    project_dir,
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    recursive = TRUE,
    full.names = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )
  csv_paths <- csv_paths[!grepl("(^|/)(renv|\\.git)/", csv_paths)]
  if (length(csv_paths) == 0L) {
    message("No CSV files found under ", project_dir)
    return(tibble::tibble())
  }
  csv_paths |>
    purrr::map(describe_csv) |>
    purrr::list_rbind()
}










Notescripts/scan_packages.R






# scan_packages.R ----
# Purpose: read renv.lock and report the R version and pinned package
# versions. A missing lockfile is reported as a finding, not an error.
# Used by: research-readme skill, Stage 4.

read_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  if (!file.exists(lock_path)) {
    return(list(found = FALSE, r_version = NA_character_, packages = tibble::tibble()))
  }
  lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_path)
  packages <- purrr::pluck(lock, "Packages", .default = list())

  packages_df <- tibble::tibble(
    package = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Package", .default = NA_character_))),
    version = unname(purrr::map_chr(packages, \(p) purrr::pluck(p, "Version", .default = NA_character_)))
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(package)

  list(
    found = TRUE,
    r_version = purrr::pluck(lock, "R", "Version", .default = NA_character_),
    packages = packages_df
  )
}

print_lockfile <- function(lock_path = "renv.lock") {
  info <- read_lockfile(lock_path)
  if (!info$found) {
    cat(
      "No lockfile found at ", lock_path, ".\n",
      "FINDING: package versions were not recorded.\n",
      "README text: **TODO: supply R version and key package versions: ",
      "not recorded; resolve before submission**\n",
      sep = ""
    )
    return(invisible(info))
  }
  cat("R version: ", info$r_version, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(info$packages, n = Inf)
  invisible(info)
}










NoteSKILL.md







---
name: research-readme
description: >-
  Writes a README.md for a research repository whose code and data accompany
  a paper. Use when asked to write a README for an analysis project, document
  a repository for a paper, or prepare code for journal submission or
  archiving (Zenodo, Figshare, OSF). Not for general software READMEs and not
  for auditing code.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Research README generator

Produces one README.md for a repository of R code and data that accompanies a
manuscript, including the metadata that journals and archives expect:
persistent identifiers, ORCIDs, funding, per-variable descriptions with units,
an explicit script run order, and a dependency record.

## Operating constraints
These hold for the whole conversation unless the user explicitly withdraws
them.
1. The only file you create or overwrite is README.md. Do not edit, rename or
   delete any other file. If you notice an apparent error in code or data,
   record it under "Open questions" in the README or report it in chat, and
   leave the file untouched.
2. Do not fabricate metadata. DOIs, ORCIDs, grant numbers, collection dates,
   units and affiliations come from the user or from a file the user points to.
   If a value is unknown, insert a placeholder (see Placeholders).
3. Automatic summaries describe; they do not interpret. Report column type,
   missing count and range. Do not state what a variable means, its unit, or
   whether a value is plausible.
4. Work conversationally and write the file directly; do not build an app.

## Before executing
Present a short numbered plan: the folder to be scanned, that only README.md
will be written, and the five stages below. Wait for the user to confirm.

## Stage 1: Project information
Collect title, abstract, DOIs (paper; archived code and data), licences,
authors with ORCIDs and affiliations, and funders with grant numbers. Read
these from CITATION.cff, codemeta.json or DESCRIPTION if present, and ask only
for what is missing. Pair each author with their own ORCID and affiliation. If
no code licence is supplied, flag it prominently and use a placeholder; do not
choose a licence for the user.

## Stage 2: Files and variable summaries
List the data and code files. For CSV files, run
describe_project_csvs() from scripts/describe_csv.R and use its output as a
scaffold. Ask the user for each column's description and unit, and for
collection dates and locations per data file. List other tabular formats
(.xlsx, .tsv) and ask the user to describe their columns by hand. Never infer
units from column names.

## Stage 3: Script order
List executable files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd). Propose a run order using numeric
prefixes (01_, 02_) as the first signal, and ask the user to confirm or
reorder; the user's order is authoritative. Collect a one-line description of
each script. Do not run any script to determine the order.

## Stage 4: R packages and versions
Run print_lockfile() from scripts/scan_packages.R.
- If a lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states the R version, says
  that versions are pinned in renv.lock, gives the restore command
  renv::restore(), and includes the package table.
- If no lockfile exists, the Dependencies section states that package versions
  were not recorded, and contains the placeholder from print_lockfile(). Do not
  guess versions or scan the installed library.

## Stage 5: Assemble, preview and reader-test
Fill references/readme_template.md. Show the rendered Markdown in chat. Then
read it as a newcomer who has only the repository and the paper: could they
find the data, restore the environment, run the scripts in order and
understand every variable? List any section still holding a placeholder. On
confirmation, write README.md to the project root.

## Stage 6: Check the README against its sources
If the project has tests/test_readme.R, run it in a fresh R session
(Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_readme.R')") and report the
output verbatim. Otherwise compare the README yourself: the R and package
versions against read_lockfile(), every numbered script against the scripts
folder, and every unit against the user's answers. Report the number of
placeholders left.

## AI declaration
State that an AI assisted in generating this README, naming the model if the
user wishes, with the date. Make no claims about AI use elsewhere in the
project unless the user states them, and then record exactly what they state.

## Placeholders
Write every unknown value as a visible placeholder, in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**

Glossary




term
definition



agent
An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.


AI declaration
A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.


claimed execution
A statement that code runs or reproduces, made without the command that was run and the output it produced. Treat it as a prediction, not evidence.


false positive
In a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly.


rung
One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.


sentinel value
A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.

Two tasks finish the record your workshop repository has built up during the day: a check that every result in a report is computed rather than typed, then a README drafted from the files you made. Both split the work the same way: you own the facts, the AI writes the text around them, and an independent check, not the AI, tells you whether to trust it.

title: Self-study: Reporting from your repository
text:
Scan a report


Goal: find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, so that each can become inline code that updates when the data change.
Start state: the template’s reports/example_report.qmd, an interim summary of the voles trial with some numbers typed in.
1. Scan it. In the R console:

source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "typed_numbers.R"))
find_typed_numbers(here::here("reports", "example_report.qmd")) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

2. Sort the hits. The scan flags five lines. Decide for each one whether it is a typed result that should be inline code, or a number that is fine as text.


Which are which

Lines 37 and 38 are typed results (the 1.53 g difference with its interval, and the mean of 29.4 g): both should be inline code. The other three can stay: the date in the YAML header (line 3), the design size of 12 per arm-by-sex combination (line 28), and “95%” in “95% CI” (line 34).

You are done when you can say which two lines are typed results and why the other three can stay.
If it goes wrong: if find_typed_numbers() is not found, check that the source() line ran without an error.









NoteHow it works: inline code, and what the scan checks





A typed number can be mistyped, or go stale when the data change, and an assistant drafting text may restate numbers it saw earlier. So every number in the prose comes from inline code: a code chunk computes the result, and the text calls it with `r round(primary$estimate, 2)`. reports/example_report.qmd, the report you scanned, does this in the first paragraph of its Results.
Your AGENTS.md asks for this; the shipped find_typed_numbers() checks it, by listing prose lines that still contain numbers outside inline code.









Notescripts/functions/typed_numbers.R






# scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R ----
# List the prose lines of a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside
# inline code, for you to review by eye. Years, design sizes and YAML values
# are flagged too, so treat each hit as a question, not an error.
find_typed_numbers <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines)
  in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1

  tibble::tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |>
    dplyr::filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |>
    dplyr::mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |>
    dplyr::filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |>
    dplyr::select(line, text)
}

text:
Part B: A README from the record
Your repository now holds most of what a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., cleaning logs, numbered scripts, a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., tests and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. A README pulls them together. The rule: the AI may only phrase facts you can trace to a file; anything else becomes a visible placeholder for you to fill.


Draft from the record, then test it


Goal: a README drafted only from your repository’s files and checked against them by a test, so that a reader can trace every statement in it to a source.
Start state: your workshop repository on main (or checkpoint-cleaning), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. Draft.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Draft README.md from these files only, naming the source of each section:
- Data dictionary, as a Markdown table whose first column is the column
  name: docs/codebook.csv
- Scripts and run order: the numbered scripts in scripts/
- Dependencies: the R version in renv.lock, and renv::restore()
- How to verify, from a terminal: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')",
  and what the tests in tests/ check
- AI declaration: docs/ai-log.md, claiming nothing beyond it
Anything these files do not give (authors, licence, DOI, a unit the codebook
leaves blank or as <unit>) becomes a placeholder in exactly this form:
**TODO: supply [field]: not provided**
Edit README.md only.
Approve the edit when asked, after reading it. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on.
2. Let the tests audit it. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

The shipped tests/test_readme.R checks the README against the files it was drafted from, and reports how many placeholders are left; How it works, after this task, lists what it checks.
3. Check the scope, log it and commit. The Git pane should show only README.md as changed. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, for example:
2026-10-20; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); drafted README.md from the repository's files; kept the draft after test_readme.R passed, placeholders still to fill
Then commit README.md and the log from the Git pane.
You are done when test_readme.R passes, the agent changed only README.md, and the README and your log line are committed.
If it goes wrong: if the agent changed any file other than README.md, select it in the Git pane and choose Revert. If the README test fails, ask Claude Code to fix only the statements the test names, and run the suite again.


Ask yourself: what did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?






NoteHow it works: the README’s sources, and what the test checks








docs/codebook.csv


numbered scripts in scripts/


tests in tests/


renv.lock


docs/ai-log.md



the only sources


Drafts README.md, with placeholders for anything missing





You trace every statement to a file


The shipped tests/test_readme.R checks the R version in renv.lock and the renv::restore() command, every numbered script, no leftover {{ tokens, and no invented unit in the data-dictionary table row for a column the codebook leaves without a unit: that row must hold a TODO instead. It also reports how many placeholders are left.









TipUsing another tool





Posit Assistant can do Part B with the same prompt. Use it in Normal mode, so it asks before each change. The checks do not change: the test suite in a fresh R session, and the Git pane.









TipStretch: audit the README by hand





The test checks the R version, the scripts, leftover tokens and blank units. Trace the statements it cannot check yourself: confirm that the AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. says no more than your log, and that each section names a source you gave it.
Before you share it, the placeholders are your to-do list. Work through licence, ORCIDs, DOI and archiving with the SORTEE checklist from Day 2, then commit.
A fuller version, with a README skill, is in Going further on the self-study page on AI-assisted code review.









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, and have an agent draft a README, trusted because a scan lists every number outside inline code, a shipped test checks the README against its sources, and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session.

Check: a scan for typed numbers; every README statement traced to a file.

Reproduce: numbers come from code, so the report updates when the data do; the README’s dependencies come from renv.lock, not from memory.

Record: the README and the AI-use log complete the record. Together with the codebook, logs, tests and lockfile, they are what a reviewer, a co-author or you in a year’s time will need. Check your institution’s and target journal’s policy on declaring AI use.

title: Self-study: Reporting from your repository
text:
Going further
This material is optional. Work through it if it is useful to you.






TipRobustness, not choice





AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice.
Run the steps yourself, and judge each answer before running it.


Enumerate, judge, run


Goal: run defensible alternatives beside your fixed primary analysis, so that you know whether your conclusion depends on the analysis choice, without letting the AI make that choice.
1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:
My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA:
mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose
versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable
analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it
estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one.
2. Judge each one yourself. Mark each alternative defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether it estimates the same quantity.
3. Run the defensible ones and report them beside the primary analysis.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R"))

voles_df <- load_voles() |>
  mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")))

specs_df <- tribble(
  ~spec,                       ~formula,
  "Primary: ANCOVA",           "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex",
  "Change score",              "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex",
  "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex",    "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex"
)

spec_results_df <- specs_df |>
  mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) {
    fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df)
    ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
    tibble(
      estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
      lower = unname(ci[1]),
      upper = unname(ci[2])
    )
  })) |>
  unnest(result)

spec_results_df



A trap in the table

In the third specification, the coefficient treatment_armHigh_dose is the High_dose effect in females only (the reference level of sex), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an “alternative” without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.

4. Log it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the alternatives it listed, and which you kept as defensible.
You are done when every alternative is marked defensible or not, with a reason, and the table beside your primary estimate holds only specifications that estimate the same quantity.








Warning



Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show.


Check your understanding: robustness
Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?

Interaction models cannot be fitted with lm()Its High_dose coefficient estimates the effect in the reference sex only, a different quantity from the primary estimandIt always gives a larger estimateRobustness tables may contain only two models











TipSimulation and parameter recovery





If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide.
Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the aims, the data-generating mechanism, the estimand, the methods and the performance measures (ADEMP). Here:


Aim: check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly.

Data-generating mechanism: 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g.

Estimand: the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g.

Method: linear model (ANCOVA), mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex.

Performance measures: bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error.

The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in Block 7: the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it.


Write, check, recover


Goal: run your analysis code on data simulated from a mechanism you wrote, so that you test it against a known answer, which real data never give.
1. Simulation code. Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function simulate_voles() returning a tibble with columns treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g and mass_post_g.
2. Check the simulated data against the specification. Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote:

set.seed(1)
sim_df <- simulate_voles()
sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex)            # 12 per cell?
sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g))
sim_df |>
  summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex))

High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted.
3. Analysis code, in a separate session. Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function estimate_high_vs_control(data) that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval.
4. Run the recovery.


Reference code


simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8,
                           effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0,
                           slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) {
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"),
    sex = c("F", "M"),
    animal = seq_len(n_per_cell)
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre),
      arm_effect = dplyr::case_when(
        treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low,
        treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high,
        .default = 0
      ),
      mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g +
        arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") +
        stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid)
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g)
}

estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}



set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 1000
true_effect <- 1.5

results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |>
  map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |>
  list_rbind()

results_df |>
  summarise(
    bias          = mean(estimate) - true_effect,
    bias_mcse     = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim),
    coverage      = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
    empirical_se  = sd(estimate)
  )

Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs.
5. Prove the check can fail. Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in Block 2:

estimate_buggy <- function(data) {
  data <- dplyr::mutate(
    data,
    treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")),
    mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g
  )
  fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data)
  ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]),
    lower = unname(ci[1]),
    upper = unname(ci[2])
  )
}

Rerun the recovery with estimate_buggy(). Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works.
6. Log it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the two functions it wrote, and what the recovery check showed.
You are done when estimate_high_vs_control() gives bias and coverage within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of their targets, and estimate_buggy() fails the same check.








Warning



What recovery does not prove. It shows that the code estimates the right quantity under the mechanism you simulated. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare empirical_se to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions.


Check your understanding: simulation
A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?

That the real data follow the simulated mechanismThat the analysis code estimates the intended quantity correctly when the data follow the simulated mechanismThat the study has adequate powerThat the model's assumptions hold for the real data











TipTranslating from SPSS, Stata or SAS





Translation with an equivalence check was the task your own agent did in Block 6: tests/test_translation.R compared its tidyverse translation with the original base R code, run side by side in R. Block 8 explains why “the same as the original” is not the same as “correct”.
From other software, export the original’s results to a file and compare the translation against those. Expect differences in defaults (missing values, quantiles, rounding); each needs a decision, not a looser tolerance.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Name the routes (3 minutes)


Goal: see exactly what reached the model provider when the agent investigated in Block 2, so that you can name every route your data take.
Start state: Claude Code running in the Terminal tab, as you left it in Block 2.






TipUsing another tool





The exercises use Claude Code. With Posit Assistant:


Exercise 1: scroll back to your Block 2 conversation in the same way. R code it ran in your session is route 4; every request also carries the names and types of your objects (route 3), though no action in the transcript shows it.

Exercise 2: use /plan for step 1 and Normal mode (/normal) for step 2. The checks are the same: the Git pane and the R console.

For GitHub Copilot, see GitHub Copilot and the remote rung in Going further.



1. Find the transcript. Scroll back in Claude Code to Block 2’s Exercise 1, where the agent read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and ran Rscript. Above each reply, Claude Code lists the actions it took. If you cleared it, re-run that prompt from Block 2.
2. Name each route in the diagram below. A file it read is route 2; the output of a command it ran is route 4; what you pasted yourself, in Exercise 2’s prompt, is route 1. Add two that no action shows: AGENTS.md, which Claude Code reads at the start of every conversation (route 2), and the context it adds itself, including your recent commit messages (route 3).
You are done when you can name every file or command output that reached the model provider.
If it goes wrong: if the transcript shows files you did not expect, or a search of the project, name those too: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below matter for confidential data.





Route 1: what you paste


Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt


any tool


Model provider




Route 2: files it reads


Copilot: open files. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: any project file they choose to read


read


Model provider




Route 3: context the tool adds itself


Claude Code: project folder, platform, date, and a snapshot of git status with recent commit messages. Posit Assistant: R version, and the names and types of your objects (not their values)


Claude Code, Posit Assistant


Model provider




Route 4: output of commands it runs


The agent runs Rscript or head data.csv, and reads what it prints


Claude Code, Posit Assistant


Model provider



Everything before an arrow reaches the model provider: any data file in the project the agent reads, and any values its code prints.








ImportantWorking with confidential data: five habits





Work on a copy. Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent’s folder.

Know your account. Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training; on Pro or Max, set /privacy-settings. Check your institution’s approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.

Deny reads of sensitive folders in /permissions, for example Read(/data/confidential/**). It stops Claude Code’s own file reads and simple commands such as cat, but not R code that opens the file itself.

Stay in Manual mode, but it does not ask before read-only commands such as head and cat, so keep confidential files out of the project (habit 1).

Describe, don’t show. names() gives column names and summary() the shape of the data; print(), glimpse() and str() show actual values.







TipHow it works: tool notes





There is no .claudeignore file, and /sandbox is not available on native Windows. Posit Assistant blocks .Renviron and .env by default, and shares the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs can still print values.











TipContext you hold in your head (instructor demonstration)





An assistant’s answer about your data is only as good as its context: it is reliable only when it has real information, such as something you pasted, a file it read, or output from a command it ran. In Block 2 you mostly pasted that information yourself; once, you let the agent fetch it. Either way, everything it uses leaves your machine.
A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your instructor asks a new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
and then, in another new chat:
Prompt (browser chat):
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision. To try it yourself, see Going further.

title: Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy
text:
Exercise 2: What can it do?
The model is the same at every rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. of the autonomy ladder; what changes is its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).: what it may do without asking. Rung 3, act with approval, is where routine work is safe: you start from a commit, so any change can be reverted; you see every edit and command first; and a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports.






NoteHow it works: the autonomy ladder





An assistant that advises leaves you to filter every change. An agent that acts removes that filter, unless you put it back: the rungs differ in how much of that filtering is left to you.
