From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool calls run without your approval; Block 6, after lunch, builds that approval step in code. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in Manual, although recent versions of Claude Code start in auto; keep Manual for confidential data. /plan can still run commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the quick reference has the rest.
Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action: in acceptEdits, for example, file commands such as cp and mv run without asking, so a cp over a raw data file needs no approval. And the higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions, which is why Block 4 writes them down.





Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)


Goal: have the agent add a column and a plot script at rung 3, then check its work with the diff and the tests, so that you trust the change because you checked it, not because the agent reported it.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Check its work from the R console and the Git pane (checking work).
1. Plan (rung 2). In Claude Code, type /clear, then:
Prompt (Claude Code):
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g) to the voles data frame itself. Create a new script
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that plots mass_change_g by
treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/ with ggsave(). Don't run
anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
Before approving, check the plan names both files, adds the column to voles itself, leaves data/raw/ alone and saves the figure to outputs/. If anything is missing, choose No, keep planning and say what to change.
2. Act, with approval (rung 3). Choose Yes, manually approve edits. It is not the first option: the first, Yes, and use auto mode, switches the approvals off. Then read each edit before you approve it. Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on.
AGENTS.md makes it ask to run git status before it edits: that only reads, so Yes is fine. It may also ask to run the new scripts with Rscript. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. For the scripts, choose No: you check the result yourself next.
3. Read the diff. Click Diff in the Git pane for each changed file and read it as you would a colleague’s work: the diff shows every change, including any you did not ask for.
4. Record. Create docs/ai-log.md (usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")) and write the first line of your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1. Don’t copy the example: put today’s date, as YYYY-MM-DD, and the model name shown above the Claude Code prompt.
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
Writing it before you test means the tests check it too.
5. Test, then commit. Restart R (Session → Restart R), so nothing left in your session can make a test pass, and run:
In the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

The tests check that mass_change_g in voles really is post minus pre, that the plot script saves a figure in outputs/ from a fresh R session, and that your log line has four parts and a real date; tests for later blocks skip. Commit the log and both scripts together (git ignores outputs/).
You are done when you have read every line of the diff, the tests show no failures, the explore and ai_log lines of the test output show their tests under OK, not S (skipped), and your first log line is committed with both scripts.
If it goes wrong: select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click Revert, then ask again more clearly. If test_explore.R says voles has no mass_change_g, the agent made the column somewhere else: ask it to add the column to voles itself. An S on explore or ai_log means its file is missing or misnamed. Out of time? Carry on: at the end of Block 4, checkpoint-skills holds this block’s files (commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked).






TipStretch: reflect on the rungs





At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff?
Payoff. What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again?









NoteAt the command line





The same checks from a terminal (after /exit, or in a second Terminal tab): git status, git diff, and Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')".











NoteThe safe vibe-coding recipe





Commit, so you start from a clean Git pane.

Protect the inputs: /permissions shows the deny rules, or you add one.

Have the checks ready: tests in tests/ before the agent starts.

Ask in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.

Run the checks: the test suite in a fresh R session.

Read the diff in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 8; the template ships the protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there.








NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, trusted because you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result.

Check: the Git pane’s diff after every agent action; the agent’s report that something “still runs” is a claim until a test confirms it.

Reproduce: work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert.

Record: your AI-use log starts here, in docs/ai-log.md.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
text:
Edit, check, verify (12 minutes)


Goal: make AGENTS.md describe your own practice and prove Claude Code loads it, so that every later conversation starts from your conventions.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab (checking work).






TipUsing another tool





The activities use Claude Code. Posit Assistant reads the same AGENTS.md: open it from the gear menu (Open project memory), or describe your conventions and run /savememory. If the canary is missing, check that you trusted the workspace. It reads skills from .agents/skills/ directly, so it needs no copy in .claude/skills/; invoke a skill by name in the same way. For other tools, see Instruction and skill files in other tools in Going further.



1. Baseline. See the starter file at work before you change it.
Prompt (Claude Code):
Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and make a quick exploratory plot
of mass_post_g by treatment arm. Show the R code in your reply; do not
create any files.
Look for the canaryA fixed line that an instruction file asks the assistant to include in its output, so that seeing the line shows the file was loaded. It does not show that the other rules were followed., # agents-md: active v1, as the first line of the code: it shows AGENTS.md was loaded.
Answer each request with plain Yes or No. Never choose an option that says don’t ask again: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Here, answer No if it asks to create or run anything: you asked only to see the code.






NoteThe starter AGENTS.md





The canary is a fixed first line the assistant is asked to put in any R code it writes, so you can see the file was loaded; asking for the code in the reply gives it somewhere to appear. The “Tests” rules ask the agent to prove its own work after every edit, which later blocks rely on.


# Project conventions: voles analysis

## Canary
When you write or edit R code, make the first line of the first code block:
# agents-md: active v1

## Structure
- Raw data live in data/raw/ and are never modified.
- Derived data go to data/derived/; figures and tables go to outputs/.
- Reusable functions live in scripts/functions/.

## R style
- Tidyverse style, native pipe |>, snake_case names, <- for assignment.
- Write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F.
- Build every path with here::here() (or here() after library(here)). Never
  use setwd() or rm(list = ls()).
- Read CSV files with readr and explicit col_types.

## Reproducibility
- Packages are managed with renv. Do not call install.packages(); ask before
  adding a package.
- Do not edit renv.lock.
- Set a seed immediately before any random step.
- Every script must run in a fresh R session.
- Before you report a task done, run each new script once with Rscript from
  the project root and report the exit status.
- Save figures with ggsave() to outputs/.

## Tests
- Before you report a task done, run Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')"
  once and paste the final summary line verbatim.
- Never edit anything in tests/fixtures/, an existing expectation or a
  tolerance to make a test pass.
- Every new function in scripts/functions/ gets a test with at least one
  known-answer case on a small tibble, including an NA; expected values are
  worked out by hand, never by running the code under test.

## Data integrity
- Never drop rows silently; state the reason for every filter in a comment.
- Report the number of observations behind every summary statistic.

## Statistics
- Label each analysis as exploratory or confirmatory.
- Never type numerical results into text; compute them in code.

## Version control
- Before you edit any file, run git status.
- If this folder is not a git repository, stop and ask me to set one up.
- If there are uncommitted changes, list them and ask whether I want to
  commit first.
- Never commit, push or change git settings unless I ask.

## Working with me
- Before changing more than one file, present a plan and wait for approval.
- Do not edit anything under data/raw/, tests/fixtures/ or .github/. The one
  exception: a skill may run tests/make_reference.R once, to capture a
  reference that does not exist yet.





2. Make it yours. Open AGENTS.md from the Files pane (or run usethis::edit_file("AGENTS.md")), and:

delete one rule you do not actually follow;
add one convention you always follow, on one line and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”).

Keep the canary and the Tests, Statistics, Version control and Working with me sections, which later blocks and tests/test_controls.R rely on. Save.






NoteWhat makes an instruction work





Use AGENTS.md for what is always true: structure, style, reproducibility rules. Instructions that work are:


One per line, and specific enough to check (“use the native pipe |>”, not “write clean code”).

True of your own code, or the model gets mixed signals.

Short, because the file loads into every request.

Added when a mistake repeats: a correction in chat is forgotten next conversation.

Not a guarantee: “never edit raw data” belongs here and in the enforced controls of Block 5.




3. Verify. Type /memory only to check that AGENTS.md is listed. Then type /clear and repeat the step 1 prompt. The canary shows the file was loaded; check the plot code against your new rule to see whether it was followed.
4. Check it with a test. Restart R (Session → Restart R), then in the R console:

testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))

Then commit AGENTS.md from the Git pane.
You are done when the canary appears, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your edited AGENTS.md is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /memory does not list AGENTS.md, delete any CLAUDE.md you created (How it works, below). If test_controls.R fails, restore the canary or the git status line; a failure in test_explore.R or test_ai_log.R is left over from Block 3. Still stuck? Compare with the checkpoint-skills branch.








NoteHow it works: which files Claude Code reads








Instruction file: loaded into every conversation


AGENTS.md: your conventions


read by


Claude Code




Skills: loaded when invoked or judged relevant


.agents/skills/<your-skill>/ (the master copy)


you copy


.claude/skills/<your-skill>/


read by


Claude Code



The course’s own skills already ship in both folders; Activity 2 shows how to copy one you write.


Claude Code reads AGENTS.md, at the repository root, at the start of every conversation because the template ships no CLAUDE.md; creating one (for example with /init) would hide your conventions. /memory lists the instruction files it loaded. Choosing one opens it in an external editor, which may be vi on macOS, so edit AGENTS.md from the Files pane instead.

title: Block 4: Instructions and skills
section: Activity 2: Write a skill and test it
text:
Activity 2: Write a skill and test it
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file. Its front matterThe block between two lines of three dashes at the top of a file, holding settings such as a skill’s name and description, or a Quarto document’s options., between two lines of three dashes, gives a name and a description, and the description is the trigger: “Use when producing a ggplot2 figure for a report, poster or paper” loads when it should; “for plots” loads erratically. The body is the procedure.


A house figure style (15 minutes)


Goal: write a skill and grade a figure made with it against your instructor’s baseline made without it, so that you judge the skill by what it changes, not by its own report.
Start state: your workshop repository on main, Git pane clean (your AGENTS.md committed), Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab.
1. The baseline, made without the skill. Your instructor runs this prompt on screen, before the skill exists; you don’t run it. Instructor: post the figure in the Zoom chat, because learners grade against it in step 4.
Prompt (Claude Code, run by your instructor):
Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles data, for a
lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_baseline.R.
2. Create the skill. In the R console, usethis::edit_file(".agents/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md") creates and opens the file. Open the box below, copy the skill into the file, and save. Read its description and six rules as you do: step 4 grades three of them.






NoteThe house-figures skill: copy this into SKILL.md





---
name: house-figures
description: >-
  Applies this project's conventions to any ggplot2 figure that will appear
  in a report, poster or paper. Use when asked to create, revise or polish a
  figure for presentation. Not for quick exploratory plots.
---

# House figure style

## Rules
1. Where any group has fewer than 30 observations, show every observation
   (jittered points or a dot plot) with a summary overlaid. Never draw a bar
   with error bars ("dynamite plot").
2. Colour categorical groups with the Okabe-Ito palette
   (grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")), and map the same
   variable to point shape so the figure works without colour.
3. Axis titles give the quantity and its unit, for example "Body mass (g)".
4. Use theme_classic(base_size = 12).
5. Show the number of observations per group on the figure.
6. Never add p-values or significance markers unless the user supplies a
   fitted model and asks for them.

## Before returning code
List which rules you applied, and any you could not apply and why.



Copy it into .claude/skills/, where Claude Code reads it:

fs::dir_copy(
  here::here(".agents", "skills", "house-figures"),
  here::here(".claude", "skills", "house-figures"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Type /skills: house-figures should be listed.






NoteHow it works: two skill folders





.agents/skills/ is the master copy, which other tools such as Posit Assistant read directly; Claude Code reads .claude/skills/, so copy the folder again whenever you change the skill. The deny rules keep the agent’s edit tools out of .claude/, so you make the copy yourself, but they do not cover .agents/skills/, so check the master copy in the Git pane too. On macOS or Linux you can link the folders instead of copying them: see Going further.
A skill suits a procedure, such as producing a publication figure or cleaning data against a codebook, and can hold scripts or templates beside SKILL.md. Its body is a procedure (when to use it, the steps, hard rules and a final check) and loads only when the skill is used, so it can be longer than AGENTS.md. Invoking it by name (/skill-name) always works. Claude Code picks up a new skill in .claude/skills/ without a restart; if /skills does not list it, type /reload-skills. For a skill that writes files, disable-model-invocation: true in the front matter makes it run only when you invoke it by name.



3. With the skill.
Prompt (Claude Code):
/house-figures Make a figure of mass_post_g by treatment_arm for the voles
data, for a lab report. Save the code as scripts/fig_house.R.
AGENTS.md makes it ask to run git status before it edits: that only reads, so Yes is fine. Read the edit before you approve it. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. So if it asks to run the new script, choose No: you run it yourself next.
4. Grade it. Restart R (Session → Restart R), run source(here::here("scripts", "fig_house.R")) and open the figure it saved in outputs/. Compare it with your instructor’s baseline on three rules you can see at a glance:


Rule
Baseline (no skill)
Your figure (with skill)



1. Raw data shown; no dynamite plot




2. Okabe-Ito colour plus shape




5. n per group shown





5. Record it. Add a line to docs/ai-log.md, as in Block 3, naming the skill and what you kept or changed in its output. Commit it with the skill (both folders) and scripts/fig_house.R.
You are done when the table is filled in from the figures you looked at, not from the agent’s list of rules it applied, and your log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if /skills does not list it, check that .claude/skills/house-figures/SKILL.md exists and its front matter starts and ends with three dashes. If no figure appears in outputs/, ask the agent to save it there with ggsave(), as AGENTS.md asks. Out of time? Commit or discard your changes in the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked, then switch to checkpoint-skills.






TipStretch: test the trigger





In a new conversation (/clear), test the trigger: “Give me a quick look at mass_post_g by arm” should not load the skill; “Make a figure of metabolic_rate_post by treatment_arm for a poster” should. Or test rule 6: ask it to “add significance stars between the groups in scripts/fig_house.R” and see whether it declines. Either way, what makes the output trustworthy is the grading in step 4, which you can repeat on every figure.
Payoff. What did the skill do for you, how long did checking it take, and would you use it for the next figure?











NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: state your conventions once, and package a procedure as a skill, trusted because the canary and tests/test_controls.R show the files are connected, and you grade the output rule by rule.

Check: a canary shows a file was loaded, not followed.

Reproduce: your AGENTS.md states the reproducibility rules; Blocks 7 and 8 check the agent kept to them.

Record: your log line from step 5.

title: Self-study: AI-assisted code review
text:
Grading the review






TipBefore you grade: what AI is, and is not, good for in code review





An AI reviewer reads every line and never tires, but it sounds equally sure whether it is right or wrong. Here is where to expect help, on the four Rs of code review (Ivimey-Cook et al., 2023):



AI capability mapped onto the four Rs

R
AI is likely to be...
Why



Reported
Useful for drafting
It can summarise what the script appears to do and flag missing documentation or undocumented exclusions. It cannot know the intended analysis unless you state it.


Run
Strong, if it can execute
An agent that runs the script in a fresh R session can show whether it runs. A chat window can only predict, and its prediction can read as though it ran the code.


Reliable
Weak
Silent semantic errors (P4 precedence, P8 sentinel, P9 incomparable models, P10 wrong family) depend on context. Expect some caught, some missed and some invented, all in the same confident tone.


Reproducible
Mixed
It can flag a missing lockfile or session record. It can confirm that results reproduce only by running the code and comparing outputs.





The rule: treat every AI finding as a claim to check, and the absence of a finding as no evidence that the problem is absent.
Run your saved review prompt on a script before you share it, and spend your own attention on the Reliable questions.
What the evidence says. Used that way, AI review is reliably good for:

summarising what an unfamiliar script does;
flagging missing documentation, unexplained filters and hard-coded paths;
finding run errors, when it can actually execute the code;
a second pair of eyes that never tires on line 300.

In software engineering, developers acted on about three-quarters of an AI reviewer’s comments but saw only minor gains in quality, and the reviewer did worse when it was not told what the code was meant to do (Cihan et al., 2025; Cihan, 2025). Nobody has measured it on analysis scripts like this one, which is what you are about to do.





Grade the machine (10 minutes)


Goal: measure the reviewer against the twelve problems you already know, so that you learn which of its findings you can trust before you rely on one.
1. Score the review. Open the answer key, the P1–P12 table under The problems revealed in the manual code-review chapter (click Solution), beside ~/ai-review/review_claude.md:


Hits: which of P1–P12 did it identify correctly?

Misses: which did it miss? Look especially at P4 (precedence) and P8 (sentinel), the silent, consequential ones.

False positives: what did it flag that is not a real problem, or describe wrongly? Each one is a false positiveIn a code review, a problem the AI reports confidently that is not real, or describes wrongly..

Execution claims: did it claim the script runs or reproduces? On what evidence?

2. Note your result. Below the review in review_claude.md, write which version of the prompt you used (with or without the 9999 line), your hit count, your most consequential miss and your most confident false positive, with line numbers, so that a second run has something to be compared with.
3. Decide. Which one finding would you act on first, and what would you check before acting on it?
4. Record it. In your workshop repository, add a line to docs/ai-log.md (date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed), with the reviewer’s hit count and its most confident false positive in the last part. Commit it from the Git pane.
You are done when every P1–P12 problem is marked hit or miss, you have listed the false positives, and your AI-log line is committed.
If it goes wrong: if your review never arrived, run it through the chat route in Using another tool; the grading works the same way.








NoteSelf-check (5 minutes)




If you ran the review both with and without the 9999 line, compare P8. Only the data and your knowledge reveal that 9999 is a code: what does that say about reviewing code without the data?
What was the reviewer’s most confident false positive, and what would acting on it have cost you?
Did the agent claim the script runs without having run it?
Back to the question at the start. Was your answer yes, because it read every line; only if you had also read it yourself; no, because you would trust your own review over the AI’s; or for Run, not for Reliable? Would you change it now?









NoteCheck · Reproduce · Record





You can now: hand a script to an AI reviewer with a prompt that makes its output checkable, trusted because you grade it against problems you already know, and treat every finding as a claim.

Check: grade every AI finding against the P1–P12 answer key; the absence of a finding is no evidence that the problem is absent.

Reproduce: a claim that the script runs counts only with the command and the output from a fresh R session; to run one yourself, see checking work.

Record: your review prompt and a line in docs/ai-log.md, both committed in your workshop repository: the tool, its hit count and its most confident false positive. An AI-assisted README for ~/ai-review is in Going further.
